Escalate, since this is a policy gap rather than a straightforward case
questions.explain:
A policy that is silent on the specific scenario (lost-in-transit) is a genuine policy gap, and the correct trigger for silence/ambiguity is escalation — not extending policy by analogy or unilaterally denying/approving a case the policy never addressed.
Not “Apply the damaged-goods policy by analogy without escalating” — Applying the damaged-goods policy by analogy extends a policy to a case it does not cover, which means inventing a resolution.
Not “Deny the request since it isn't explicitly authorized” — Denying because the exception is not authorised assumes silence means no, when the policy gives no answer on lost goods.
Not “Approve the request since it isn't explicitly denied” — Approving because nothing denies it assumes silence means yes, so the agent would make up a decision the policy never gave.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline validates against a JSON schema and a required field, purchase_order_number, fails validation because it's missing. Investigation confirms the source invoice genuinely never included a PO number. What's the correct interpretation?
options: Increase max_tokens and retry
This retry is unlikely to succeed since the information doesn't exist in the source; the field should be nullable instead of required
Retry with the same prompt; missing-field errors are always retry-fixable
The schema needs a stricter type constraint
questions.explain:
The invoice genuinely never had a PO number, so no amount of retrying manufactures data that isn't in the source; the fix is upstream, making the field nullable. Increasing max_tokens or retrying the same prompt can't invent missing information, and a stricter type constraint doesn't address absence.
Not “Increase max_tokens and retry” — More max_tokens cannot create a PO number that the invoice never contained.
Not “Retry with the same prompt; missing-field errors are always retry-f…” — Missing-field errors are only retry-fixable when the data exists in the source. Here it does not, so the same prompt fails again.
Not “The schema needs a stricter type constraint” — A stricter type constraint does not help when the value is simply absent. Making the field nullable is what fits.

questions.q: A validation-retry loop needs to correct a structural JSON error (a nested array flattened incorrectly) on the second attempt. What should the follow-up prompt include?
options: Nothing — tool_use with schemas should never produce structural errors, so no retry should be needed
The original document, the failed extraction output, and the specific validation error describing the structural mismatch
A brand-new, unrelated example document
Only a repeated instruction to "format correctly this time"
questions.explain:
A structural error like a flattened array is retry-fixable, but only if the follow-up gives new information to correct against: the original document, the failed output, and the specific validation error. Repeating "format correctly" or an unrelated example provides no diagnostic signal, and assuming schema-enforced tools can never produce structural errors is false.
Not “Nothing — tool_use with schemas should never produce structural e…” — Schema-enforced output still allows structural mistakes such as a flattened nested array, so a retry can well be needed.
Not “A brand-new, unrelated example document” — An unrelated example document gives no information about this specific failure, so the model cannot correct it.
Not “Only a repeated instruction to "format correctly this time"” — Repeating "format correctly" without showing what was wrong gives the model nothing concrete to fix.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes what tool_use with a JSON schema does and does not guarantee?
options: It guarantees semantic correctness but not syntactic validity
It guarantees syntactic (schema-compliant) validity but not semantic correctness (e.g., values landing in the wrong field or totals not summing)
It guarantees neither, and offers no benefit over plain-text JSON output
It guarantees both syntactic validity and semantic correctness of extracted values
questions.explain:
tool_use with a schema guarantees the output parses and matches the schema's structure (syntactic validity) but cannot verify that values are semantically correct, e.g., a total that doesn't sum or a value in the wrong field. D overclaims that semantic correctness is also guaranteed, which is exactly the gap a calculated_total vs. stated_total check exists to catch.
Not “It guarantees semantic correctness but not syntactic validity” — This reverses the guarantee. A schema ensures valid structure, but it cannot ensure values are semantically correct.
Not “It guarantees neither, and offers no benefit over plain-text JSON o…” — It does provide a benefit: output reliably parses and matches the schema, which plain-text JSON does not guarantee.
Not “It guarantees both syntactic validity and semantic correctness of e…” — It does not guarantee semantic correctness. Values can sit in the wrong field or totals can fail to add up while the JSON stays valid.

questions.q: An enum field for expense category needs to remain useful even as new, unanticipated categories appear in documents over time. What schema pattern handles this well?
options: Multiple boolean flags, one per possible category
A required string field with no enum constraint at all
A closed enum with no fallback option
An enum with an "other" value paired with a free-text category_detail field
questions.explain:
Pairing an "other" enum value with a free-text category_detail field lets the schema absorb novel categories without breaking validation while still capturing detail. A closed enum breaks on any new category, dropping the enum sacrifices validation entirely, and per-category booleans can't scale to unanticipated categories.
Not “Multiple boolean flags, one per possible category” — One boolean per category cannot represent categories nobody has anticipated and becomes unwieldy as categories grow.
Not “A required string field with no enum constraint at all” — An unconstrained string gives up validation, allowing inconsistent spellings and values that are hard to group.
Not “A closed enum with no fallback option” — A closed enum with no fallback would fail or misclassify whenever a new category appears in a document.

questions.q: Which best describes the purpose of a detected_pattern field attached to each automated finding in a review or extraction pipeline?
options: It determines whether tool_choice should be "auto" or "any"
It stores the model's self-reported confidence
It enables systematic downstream analysis of which specific patterns trigger findings, useful for spotting recurring false-positive causes
It flags whether a finding is retryable
questions.explain:
Tagging findings with the specific pattern that triggered them turns one-off fixes into an aggregate signal for spotting recurring false-positive causes. It's unrelated to tool_choice, isn't a confidence score, and doesn't indicate retryability.
Not “It determines whether tool_choice should be "auto" or "any"” — Choosing between "auto" and "any" is made per request, and it is not determined by a tag on findings.
Not “It stores the model's self-reported confidence” — A confidence score is a separate field. detected_pattern records what triggered the finding, not how sure the model was.
Not “It flags whether a finding is retryable” — Whether a finding can be retried is a different property, and detected_pattern carries no information about retryability.

questions.q: Few-shot examples are added to an extraction prompt specifically to handle documents with varied structures — some using inline citations, others using bibliographies, some embedding methodology details inline versus in a separate section. What is the main benefit?
options: They demonstrate correct handling of structural variety, helping the model generalize to formats not explicitly shown
They guarantee the model will never omit a field
They eliminate the need for a JSON schema entirely
Few-shot examples primarily reduce token usage
questions.explain:
Showing a few examples across genuinely different document structures teaches the underlying judgment (how to locate methodology or citations regardless of layout), letting the model generalize to formats not explicitly shown. Few-shot examples don't guarantee zero omissions, don't replace schema enforcement, and typically add tokens rather than reduce them.
Not “They guarantee the model will never omit a field” — Few-shot examples improve behaviour but cannot guarantee that a field is never omitted.
Not “They eliminate the need for a JSON schema entirely” — Examples do not replace schema enforcement. The schema still guarantees structure, while examples guide judgment on varied layouts.
Not “Few-shot examples primarily reduce token usage” — Examples add tokens to the prompt, so reducing token usage is not their purpose.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline is being scaled from a 20-document pilot to a 5,000-document production run using the Message Batches API. What should happen before the full run?
options: Switch to synchronous calls for the full run instead of batch
Submit all 5,000 immediately to save time
Refine the prompt against a smaller sample set first to maximize first-pass success and reduce costly iterative resubmission at scale
Skip validation entirely for the full run since the pilot already passed
questions.explain:
At 5,000-document scale with batch turnaround up to 24 hours and no latency SLA, discovering a prompt flaw only after the full run is enormously costly, so refining against a smaller sample first maximizes first-pass success. Submitting everything immediately or skipping validation both forfeit the cheap chance to catch systematic errors early, and abandoning batch throws away the reason for using it.
Not “Switch to synchronous calls for the full run instead of batch” — Switching to synchronous calls gives up the cost savings that motivated batch, when the better step is refining the prompt on a sample first.
Not “Submit all 5,000 immediately to save time” — Submitting all 5,000 at once risks a systematic prompt flaw only surfacing after a costly full run, with up to a day's turnaround.
Not “Skip validation entirely for the full run since the pilot already p…” — Skipping validation because a 20-document pilot passed assumes the pilot represents 5,000 varied documents, so systematic errors may go uncaught.

questions.q: A stakeholder wants to know if a 96% aggregate extraction accuracy is good enough to safely reduce human review across the board. What should be checked first?
options: The average length of the source documents
Accuracy broken down by document type and by individual field, since aggregate numbers can mask segment-specific failure
Whether --json-schema was used during extraction
Nothing further; 96% aggregate is a strong number on its own
questions.explain:
A 96% aggregate can hide a document type or field performing far worse, so only a by-type, by-field breakdown reveals whether review can safely be reduced broadly or only for specific segments. Document length and whether a schema flag was used don't address the masking risk, and accepting the aggregate at face value is the exact mistake stratified analysis prevents.
Not “The average length of the source documents” — Average source document length says nothing about whether accuracy holds across every document type and field.
Not “Whether --json-schema was used during extraction” — Whether --json-schema was used affects output structure, not whether the 96% hides segments performing poorly.
Not “Nothing further; 96% aggregate is a strong number on its own” — A 96% aggregate can mask a document type or field performing much worse, so it is not enough to justify reducing review.

questions.q: Field-level confidence scores are used to route low-confidence extractions to human reviewers with limited capacity. What should determine the confidence threshold used for routing?
options: Calibration against a labeled validation set so the threshold maps to actual accuracy
The number of required fields in the schema
The size of the review team, independent of accuracy data
An arbitrary round number chosen for simplicity
questions.explain:
A threshold is only meaningful if tied to what confidence level actually predicts correctness, which requires calibration against labeled ground truth. Sizing it to schema field count, team headcount, or an arbitrary round number fits the threshold to convenience rather than actual error risk.
Not “The number of required fields in the schema” — Field count has no connection to how reliable a given confidence score is, so it is not a sound basis for the threshold.
Not “The size of the review team, independent of accuracy data” — Team size sets capacity, not the point where confidence predicts errors, so a threshold based on it ignores actual accuracy.
Not “An arbitrary round number chosen for simplicity” — An arbitrary round number has no link to real error rates, so it could send the wrong items to reviewers.

questions.q: Two extracted values for the same metric conflict because they come from two source documents published a year apart, representing a genuine change over time rather than an error. What structured field, if present, would have prevented this from being misread as a contradiction?
options: Publication or data-collection date fields on each extracted value
isRetryable
tool_choice
errorCategory
questions.explain:
Attaching a publication or data-collection date to each extracted value lets downstream synthesis recognize a legitimate change over time rather than flag a contradiction. isRetryable, tool_choice, and errorCategory are extraction-mechanics fields that say nothing about when the underlying fact was true.
Not “isRetryable” — isRetryable describes whether a failed call can be tried again, and says nothing about when a value was measured.
Not “tool_choice” — tool_choice controls how the model is made to call tools and carries no timing information about the underlying facts.
Not “errorCategory” — errorCategory classifies failures. Both values were extracted successfully, so it cannot explain an apparent conflict.

questions.q: Which best describes when retrying a failed extraction is NOT likely to help?
options: When the required information is genuinely absent from the source document entirely
When the model swapped two adjacent fields
When the validation error indicates a structural/format mismatch that's fixable through clearer instructions
When a nested array was flattened incorrectly
questions.explain:
Retrying only helps when there's new information or clearer instruction to converge on; if the value was never in the source document, no retry can invent it. Swapped fields, flattened arrays, and structural/format mismatches are exactly the error class a specific validation error message can fix.
Not “When the model swapped two adjacent fields” — Swapped adjacent fields are a mistake that a specific validation error can point out, so retrying with that feedback is likely to help.
Not “When the validation error indicates a structural/format mismatch th…” — A format mismatch that clearer instructions can fix is the kind of error a retry with the validation message can correct.
Not “When a nested array was flattened incorrectly” — A wrongly flattened nested array is a structural error that a retry with the specific error can typically correct.

questions.q: An extraction schema requires stated_total and also asks the model to compute calculated_total from the line items. What is the purpose of including both?
options: Enabling downstream detection of semantic mismatches (the two numbers disagree) that schema validation alone wouldn't catch
Redundancy for its own sake
To satisfy tool_choice: "any" requirements
To reduce the number of required fields elsewhere
questions.explain:
Requiring both the stated and a model-computed total creates a downstream check schema validation alone can't perform: if the two disagree, something is semantically wrong even in well-formed JSON. It isn't redundancy for its own sake, unrelated to tool_choice, and doesn't reduce required fields elsewhere.
Not “Redundancy for its own sake” — Comparing the two totals is not redundancy for its own sake. It lets downstream checks detect a semantic mismatch that the schema cannot.
Not “To satisfy tool_choice: "any" requirements” — tool_choice: "any" concerns forcing a tool call and has no link to why both totals are requested.
Not “To reduce the number of required fields elsewhere” — Asking for both totals adds a field rather than reducing required fields elsewhere, so that is not its purpose.

questions.q: A synthesis-style extraction task combines financial figures, narrative commentary, and technical specifications from a single source document into one structured output. How should each content type be rendered in the final structured output?
options: Only the financial figures should be kept; other content types should be dropped
Appropriately to its type — e.g., financial data as tables, narrative as prose, technical specs as structured lists
Uniformly as plain paragraphs regardless of content type
Entirely as a single JSON blob with no formatting distinctions
questions.explain:
Financial figures, narrative, and specs carry different information shapes, and collapsing them into one uniform format throws away structure that's cheap to preserve and useful downstream. Dropping non-financial content discards real information, and forcing everything into plain paragraphs or an undifferentiated JSON blob both erase distinctions the source document actually has.
Not “Only the financial figures should be kept; other content types shou…” — Dropping the narrative and technical content throws away useful information the task asks to combine.
Not “Uniformly as plain paragraphs regardless of content type” — Making everything plain paragraphs erases the useful structure of tables and lists, which the source and downstream use rely on.
Not “Entirely as a single JSON blob with no formatting distinctions” — A single undifferentiated JSON blob loses the distinctions between content types, making the output harder to read and use.

questions.q: Your resolution agent has a PreToolUse hook that blocks process_refund calls exceeding $750. Logs show the hook is working correctly — every blocked refund is correctly identified. However, first-contact resolution dropped 12% in the last month. Investigation reveals that many customers' refund requests between $400–$750 are now being incorrectly escalated even though policy allows them, and the agent is calling escalate_to_human before ever attempting process_refund. What's the issue?
options: The threshold is set too high; lower it to $500 to prevent false escalations
The hook is correct, but the agent's premature escalation suggests the process_refund tool description doesn't make clear that it handles amounts up to the threshold
The hook should use PostToolUse instead of PreToolUse to allow the refund attempt first
Replace the hook with a system-prompt instruction that lists the threshold explicitly
questions.explain:
The hook enforcement is doing its job; the defect is upstream. The agent escalates *before* attempting process_refund because it doesn't understand the tool can handle refunds up to $750 — that's a description problem, not a hook problem. Lowering the threshold doesn't touch the premature-escalation behavior, and PostToolUse would let the over-threshold refund attempt happen before blocking it, which is worse, not better.
Not “The threshold is set too high; lower it to $500 to prevent false es…” — Lowering the threshold to $500 would block even more legitimate refunds and does nothing about the agent escalating before it ever tries process_refund. The hook already works as intended.
Not “The hook should use PostToolUse instead of PreToolUse to allow …” — PostToolUse fires after the tool has run, so an over-limit refund would already be executed before it could be blocked. That is worse, and it does not change the early escalation.
Not “Replace the hook with a system-prompt instruction that lists the th…” — Replacing the hook with a prompt instruction trades a deterministic limit for a probabilistic one, and it does not explain why the agent escalates without trying the refund.

questions.q: Your support agent integrates with two MCP tools: lookup_legacy_order (for orders from 2+ years ago) and lookup_recent_order (for current orders). Both return {"isError": true, "message": "Lookup failed"} for any failure — timeout, invalid order ID, or permission denied. The agent sometimes retries timeouts unnecessarily and sometimes gives up on permission errors that should escalate instead. What's the root cause?
options: The tools need better descriptions so the agent picks the correct one first
The tool results lack structured error metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable); the agent can't distinguish a retryable timeout from a non-retryable permission failure
The agent should use tool_choice: "any" to force it to select one of the two tools
The MCP server is responding too quickly; add artificial delays so the model sees a timeout signal
questions.explain:
A flat isError: true with no category tells the agent nothing about whether to retry, escalate, or move on. errorCategory and isRetryable let it distinguish a retry-safe timeout from a permission failure that needs escalation instead. Better descriptions fix tool *selection*, not recovery after a call has already failed.
Not “The tools need better descriptions so the agent picks the correct o…” — Better descriptions help the agent choose between the two lookup tools. The problem here is what happens after a call fails, when every failure looks identical.
Not “The agent should use tool_choice: "any" to force it to select one…” — tool_choice: "any" only forces some tool to be called. It gives the agent no way to tell a retryable timeout from a permission failure.
Not “The MCP server is responding too quickly; add artificial delays so …” — Adding artificial delays would not tell the model why a call failed, and it makes the system slower. The tools need to report the failure type.

questions.q: A customer named "Utkarsh Agarwal" matches 5 accounts in the system: four inactive, one active from last month. The agent selects the active account without asking for clarification. That account belongs to a different customer with the same name — the agent processes a $340 refund for the wrong person. What's the correct behavior when a lookup returns multiple matches?
options: Pick the most recently active account, since it's the most likely match
Ask the customer for an additional identifier before proceeding
Process the request against all matching accounts and let the customer confirm afterward
Escalate immediately, since multi-match lookups are inherently too ambiguous to handle autonomously
questions.explain:
Ambiguous multi-match lookups should never be resolved by a heuristic like recency; ask for another identifier (email, phone, order number) to disambiguate safely. Guessing based on recent activity is exactly the anti-pattern that caused the wrong-customer refund here.
Not “Pick the most recently active account, since it's the most likely m…” — Recent activity does not show which account the caller actually owns, and this exact heuristic caused the wrong-customer refund in the scenario.
Not “Process the request against all matching accounts and let the custo…” — Processing the request against every match would act on accounts belonging to other people, and a later confirmation cannot reverse those actions.
Not “Escalate immediately, since multi-match lookups are inherently too …” — Multiple matches do not make a case too ambiguous to handle. Asking for one more identifier resolves it without involving a human.

questions.q: A customer messages: "I need to return a wireless headset AND I'm being charged twice for my subscription." The agent decomposes this into two concerns and investigates the billing dispute first, finding a duplicate charge and auto-refunding $15. Only afterward does it address the return, discovering the headset was purchased as part of a non-refundable promotional bundle 45 days ago, and escalates the return. The customer is upset because the billing refund had already gone through before the return was found to be ineligible. What went wrong?
options: The agent should have escalated both concerns immediately instead of attempting autonomous resolution
The agent should have investigated eligibility/prerequisites across both concerns before issuing any refund, not resolve one item to completion before even starting to investigate the other
The agent picked the wrong concern to address first; pure ordering shouldn't matter otherwise
The agent needed stronger prompting to handle multi-concern messages
questions.explain:
The failure isn't that the agent worked on the wrong concern first — it's that it fully executed one concern (issuing a refund) before checking prerequisites relevant to the other. Eligibility and prerequisite checks across all concerns should happen before any high-stakes action is taken, precisely because refunds are hard to unwind once issued.
Not “The agent should have escalated both concerns immediately instead o…” — Both concerns were within the agent's ability. The flaw was the order of actions, not that autonomous handling was attempted, so escalating everything is excessive.
Not “The agent picked the wrong concern to address first; pure ordering …” — The order of addressing the concerns is not the real defect. Even with a different order, a refund issued before checking the other item's eligibility could cause the same surprise.
Not “The agent needed stronger prompting to handle multi-concern messages” — Stronger prompting is a probabilistic fix. The structural problem is issuing an irreversible refund before checking prerequisites that relate to the other concern.

questions.q: Your agent has access to four tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. Metrics show 65% of cases that call escalate_to_human are actually routine refunds that could have been auto-resolved, while autonomous resolution succeeds 78% of the time on the clear-cut cases it does attempt. The agent is over-escalating standard cases while handling some genuinely ambiguous ones autonomously. What's the most direct structural fix?
options: Rewrite tool descriptions to be more explicit about when to escalate
Remove get_customer and lookup_order from the toolset, leaving only process_refund and escalate_to_human, to reduce tool confusion
Keep all four tools, but restrict escalate_to_human so it can only be called after both get_customer and lookup_order have already returned substantive data
Rewrite the system prompt's escalation criteria in more detail
questions.explain:
Restricting when escalate_to_human can be called — only after get_customer and lookup_order have already returned something substantive — directly targets premature escalation without removing tools the agent still needs for legitimate investigation. Stripping investigative tools would make *every* case harder to resolve, not just the over-escalated ones.
Not “Rewrite tool descriptions to be more explicit about when to escalate” — More explicit descriptions only nudge behaviour. They do not stop the agent from calling escalate_to_human before it has investigated, which is the structural gap here.
Not “Remove get_customer and lookup_order from the toolset, leaving …” — Removing the investigative tools leaves the agent unable to gather the information needed to resolve cases, making every case harder to handle, not just the over-escalated ones.
Not “Rewrite the system prompt's escalation criteria in more detail” — More detailed escalation criteria in the system prompt are followed only probabilistically, so premature escalation would still happen.

questions.q: A 12-turn conversation about a disputed order involves: the customer claims a $60 charge on order #7742, the agent verifies the charge exists, and by turn 8 a running summary has condensed the details down to "customer disputes a charge." On turn 11, the customer references "like the $50 I got back last month for the same vendor," but the agent has lost the original $60 figure in the summarized history and asks the customer to repeat the amount. What fix would prevent this?
options: Never summarize; keep the full raw conversation history in every turn
Maintain a persistent "case facts" block (amount, order ID, dates) carried alongside every message, outside the narrative summary that gets condensed
Increase the context window size
Lower the temperature to make behavior more consistent across long conversations
questions.explain:
A persistent case-facts block (amount, order ID, dates) carried alongside the narrative prevents exactly this kind of detail loss during summarization. Keeping the full raw history forever avoids the problem but doesn't scale, and neither context-window size nor temperature address progressive detail loss from summarization itself.
Not “Never summarize; keep the full raw conversation history in every turn” — Keeping the entire raw history in every turn avoids the loss but does not scale, and it discards the benefits of summarising long conversations.
Not “Increase the context window size” — A larger window does not change what the summary keeps. The $60 figure was dropped by summarisation, not by running out of space.
Not “Lower the temperature to make behavior more consistent across long …” — Temperature governs randomness and does not prevent summarisation from stripping details such as the amount and order number.

questions.q: Your policy requires that refunds under $100 can be auto-approved, but refunds of $100+ must first have the customer's identity verified via get_customer. Some get_customer calls fail due to network timeouts, and the agent currently retries the same call several times before eventually calling escalate_to_human. You want to *guarantee* that process_refund can never be called for $100+ unless get_customer has already returned a verified ID in the conversation — not just make it likely. Which mechanism enforces this?
options: A PostToolUse hook that appends a reminder to the agent after process_refund succeeds, noting that identity should have been verified first
A PreToolUse hook that blocks process_refund for amounts at or above $100 until a verified-ID flag from get_customer is present in the conversation
A PostToolUse hook that normalizes get_customer results into a canonical verified/unverified format
A system-prompt instruction stating that identity verification is required before large refunds
questions.explain:
Only a PreToolUse hook can block process_refund *before* it executes, which is what "guarantee" requires here. A PostToolUse hook fires after the refund has already gone through, and a prompt instruction is followed probabilistically, not deterministically — exactly the gap the team wants closed.
Not “A PostToolUse hook that appends a reminder to the agent after `pr…” — A PostToolUse reminder arrives after process_refund has already succeeded, so it can only note the mistake, not prevent it.
Not “A PostToolUse hook that normalizes get_customer results into a …” — Normalising get_customer output does not stop process_refund from running, and a PostToolUse hook acts after the fact, so it guarantees nothing about ordering.
Not “A system-prompt instruction stating that identity verification is r…” — A prompt instruction is followed probabilistically, which the team has said is not enough, since they want a guarantee.

questions.q: Your team escalates any case that reaches 8 conversational turns, on the theory that long conversations indicate complex cases. Data shows this rule escalates many routine multi-step refunds (identity verification + refund processing routinely takes 6–8 turns) while some genuinely ambiguous policy-exception cases stay in autonomous resolution because they happen to resolve in fewer turns. What's wrong with using turn count as an escalation signal?
options: It's actually a reasonable proxy for complexity; just raise the threshold to 12 turns

Turn count is orthogonal to case complexity — the same routine workflow can take 3 turns or 10 depending on how the customer communicates. Escalation should trigger on an actual policy gap or ambiguity the agent can't resolve, not on conversation length
Escalate based on customer sentiment instead of turn count
Add a per-turn confidence score and escalate when the average drops below a threshold
questions.explain:
Turn count doesn't track complexity — the same routine workflow can span very different numbers of turns depending on the customer's communication style. Escalation should be triggered by an actual unresolved ambiguity or policy gap, not by how long the conversation happened to run.
Not “It's actually a reasonable proxy for complexity; just raise the thr…” — Raising the turn threshold to 12 keeps a signal that does not track complexity. Routine workflows would still be escalated or missed based on how long the customer takes.
Not “Escalate based on customer sentiment instead of turn count” — Customer sentiment is another unreliable proxy for case complexity, and it would escalate routine cases just because the customer sounded annoyed.
Not “Add a per-turn confidence score and escalate when the average drops…” — An average of self-reported per-turn confidence rests on poorly calibrated scores, so it would not reliably separate complex cases from routine ones.

questions.q: A case is escalated to a human with a structured handoff containing: customer ID, disputed order number, refund amount, and a recommended action ("Approve $85 refund, order is within the 30-day window"). The human approves the refund. Two days later, the customer says the refund never arrived and demands to know why the agent didn't just process it. Investigation shows the AI agent never actually called process_refund — it only reasoned that a human should approve one. What element is missing from the escalation structure that would have prevented this confusion?
options: The full unedited transcript, so the human can re-trace the entire investigation themselves
A field documenting exactly what the agent already attempted, and explicitly stating that no refund action was taken by the agent itself — only a recommendation
The customer's original message, verbatim, to confirm the request was genuine
A confidence score, so the human knows how uncertain the agent was
questions.explain:
The handoff records *what the agent recommended* but never states *whether the agent itself took any action*. Without an explicit field for "attempted actions" (and confirmation that no refund was actually executed), a human reviewer has no way to know the recommendation still requires their own action to complete — which is exactly the gap that led to the refund never happening.
Not “The full unedited transcript, so the human can re-trace the entire …” — A full transcript makes the human re-trace everything and still does not state whether the agent itself acted, so the confusion would remain.
Not “The customer's original message, verbatim, to confirm the request w…” — The original message confirms what the customer asked for but not what the agent did or did not do, so the gap about the missing refund remains.
Not “A confidence score, so the human knows how uncertain the agent was” — A confidence score tells the human how unsure the agent was, but nothing about whether any refund action had actually been taken.

questions.q: A .claude/settings.json hook is configured with matcher: "Bash", type: "command", intended to block any Bash invocation that references production credentials. The hook's script correctly detects and prints the matched credential key name in logs, but Bash commands referencing those credentials still execute anyway. What's the most likely fix?
options: Change the matcher from "Bash" to a regex like "Bash.*" so it matches the tool name correctly
Make sure the hook's script actually exits with a non-zero exit code when it detects a match — printing a log line alone does not block the tool call
Move the hook from PreToolUse to PostToolUse, since that's when the final decision on the Bash call is made
Add a separate {"type": "approval"} hook entry alongside the existing command hook
questions.explain:
A command hook only blocks a tool call if its script exits non-zero; printing a detection message to logs has no effect on the tool-use decision itself. The matcher syntax is fine as written, PostToolUse would run after the Bash command has already executed, and "approval" isn't a valid hook type.
Not “Change the matcher from "Bash" to a regex like "Bash.*" so it m…” — The matcher "Bash" already matches the Bash tool. The hook fires and finds the credential, so the matching syntax is not the cause.
Not “Move the hook from PreToolUse to PostToolUse, since that's when…” — PostToolUse runs after the command has already executed, so it cannot prevent the Bash call from running.
Not “Add a separate {"type": "approval"} hook entry alongside the exis…” — approval is not a valid hook type, so adding such an entry would not block anything.

questions.q: A developer needs to add one new database index to speed up a slow, already-diagnosed query. The change touches one file, is 5–10 lines, and the team has already agreed on which index to add. Should this go through plan mode first?
options: Yes — plan mode should review the indexing strategy before any implementation
No — plan mode is built for exploring multiple valid approaches on complex, multi-file work; a single well-understood, already-decided change doesn't need that overhead
Yes — plan mode is required to check the index doesn't affect other queries
No, but only because this is a bug fix; any new feature work should always go through plan mode
questions.explain:
Plan mode earns its overhead on multi-file work with several genuinely valid approaches; a single-file, already-decided, five-to-ten-line change gets nothing extra from a planning pass and only adds latency. Feature-vs-bugfix isn't the relevant distinction — task complexity and decision-ambiguity are.
Not “Yes — plan mode should review the indexing strategy before any impl…” — A single 5-10 line change that the team already decided on has no strategy to review, so a planning pass only adds delay.
Not “Yes — plan mode is required to check the index doesn't affect other…” — Plan mode is not a requirement for checking effects on other queries, and the change is small and already agreed, so this is not a reason to plan.
Not “No, but only because this is a bug fix; any new feature work should…” — Whether the work is a bug fix or a feature is not the deciding factor. Complexity and the number of valid approaches are what matter.

questions.q: A /release-notes skill converts raw commit messages into user-facing changelog entries. Across five runs on similar commits, the results vary: sometimes technical jargon that should be simplified is kept as-is, other times breaking-change details are oversimplified into vague language. The prompt already says "write for a non-technical audience while preserving important details." What's the most effective next fix?
options: Add a stronger prompt clause: "Always balance technical accuracy with customer-friendly language"
Add 2–3 concrete before/after examples that show exactly which terms to simplify, which details must survive simplification (e.g., breaking changes), and how each should be phrased
Generate five variants per commit and have a human manually pick the best one each time
Split the skill into two skills — one for breaking changes, one for routine fixes — to reduce the range of cases each has to handle
questions.explain:
When the same category of transformation produces inconsistent results despite clear prose instructions, concrete before/after examples that pin down the exact boundary (which terms to simplify, what must survive simplification) are more effective than further prose, manual cherry-picking, or splitting the task, none of which resolve the underlying ambiguity in what "customer-friendly but accurate" actually means here.
Not “Add a stronger prompt clause: "Always balance technical accuracy wi…” — Another prose clause restates the same vague balance between accuracy and simplicity, so the variation between runs would continue.
Not “Generate five variants per commit and have a human manually pick th…” — Choosing from five variants by hand adds recurring human effort and never settles what the right boundary is.
Not “Split the skill into two skills — one for breaking changes, one for…” — Splitting the skill narrows the cases each handles but does not define which terms to simplify or which details must survive.

questions.q: A convention that all new database migrations follow a specific naming/structure pattern needs to apply to files under both migrations/ and tools/legacy-migrations/ — two directories with no other relationship. What's the most maintainable way to enforce this?
options: Create migrations/CLAUDE.md and tools/legacy-migrations/CLAUDE.md, each repeating the same convention
Create a single .claude/rules/migrations.md with paths: ["**/migrations/**/*.sql", "**/legacy-migrations/**/*.sql"] frontmatter
Add a "Migration" section to the root CLAUDE.md
Build a custom /migration-check skill that developers must remember to run before creating a migration file
questions.explain:
A single glob-scoped .claude/rules/ file with paths covering both migration directories applies the convention wherever migration files live, without duplicating content across directory-level CLAUDE.md files or bloating the root CLAUDE.md with a rule that's only relevant to a subset of files.
Not “Create migrations/CLAUDE.md and `tools/legacy-migrations/CLAUDE.m…” — Repeating the same convention in two directory CLAUDE.md files duplicates content that can drift apart and ties it to specific locations.
Not “Add a "Migration" section to the root CLAUDE.md” — A root CLAUDE.md section loads the migration convention for every task, including those with no migration files, bloating the context.
Not “Build a custom /migration-check skill that developers must rememb…” — A manually run skill depends on developers remembering to invoke it, so the convention would be skipped whenever someone forgets.

questions.q: A developer spends 90 minutes exploring a legacy data-processing module before asking Claude to write a new version of a core function. The generated code is syntactically clean and passes a quick smoke test, but it silently violates a constraint documented in a code comment the developer read in the first 20 minutes of exploration — a comment Claude never referenced when generating the new version. What should have been set up during the exploration phase to prevent this?
options: Use the Explore subagent to keep verbose discovery output out of the main context, and have Claude maintain a scratchpad file recording critical constraints found along the way
Start a brand-new session for the implementation step so old exploration context doesn't interfere
Ask for a larger context window so nothing needs to be dropped during the session
Switch to plan mode specifically to review the findings before implementation begins
questions.explain:
A scratchpad file capturing constraints discovered during exploration — paired with the Explore subagent to keep the verbose search process itself out of the main context — is the direct fix for exactly this failure mode: a constraint noticed early gets silently dropped by the time implementation happens. A fresh session or a bigger context window don't capture and resurface the constraint; they just change how much gets forgotten and when.
Not “Start a brand-new session for the implementation step so old explor…” — A fresh session for implementation loses everything learned during exploration, including the constraint, and does not record it anywhere.
Not “Ask for a larger context window so nothing needs to be dropped duri…” — A larger context window does not make Claude re-check a comment read early on, and it does not record the constraint anywhere to be revisited.
Not “Switch to plan mode specifically to review the findings before impl…” — Plan mode before implementation does not capture constraints found earlier, so a review of findings is only as good as what was written down.

questions.q: An automated PR review pipeline deliberately uses a fresh, independent Claude Code instance to review code rather than reusing the session that generated the fix. A reviewer complains that this independent reviewer still misses a subtle cross-function interaction bug that seems obvious once pointed out. Is the independent-instance design itself the problem?
options: Yes — the independent instance should be given the original session's generation reasoning so it has more context to work with

No — the point of an independent instance is specifically to avoid the generation session's own reasoning bias, which otherwise makes it less likely to challenge its own prior decisions; this particular miss is a separate issue, not evidence the pattern is wrong
Yes — both steps should run in the same session so context carries over cleanly
No, but the reviewer instance should switch models between runs to add perspective diversity
questions.explain:
This is intentional design, not a bug: a session that generated the fix retains its own reasoning and is measurably less likely to challenge its own prior decisions, so an independent review session is used specifically to avoid that bias. This particular miss doesn't invalidate the pattern — it's a separate reliability gap. Giving the reviewer the generation reasoning or merging the two steps would reintroduce the exact bias the design is meant to avoid.
Not “Yes — the independent instance should be given the original session…” — Passing along the generation reasoning would bring back the bias that makes the generating session reluctant to challenge its own decisions.
Not “Yes — both steps should run in the same session so context carries …” — Running both steps in the same session reintroduces the very bias that an independent reviewer is meant to avoid.
Not “No, but the reviewer instance should switch models between runs to …” — Switching models between runs does not address why one subtle miss happened, and it is not the purpose of using an independent instance.

questions.q: A skill's SKILL.md sets context: fork and argument-hint: "Describe the target API". Invoking it with no arguments prompts the developer to describe the target API. Invoking it with a description already supplied as an argument runs the skill silently, with no follow-up prompt. Is this the correct, documented behavior of argument-hint?
options: No — argument-hint should always prompt regardless of whether arguments were supplied; the missing prompt is a bug
Yes — argument-hint is autocomplete guidance shown when no arguments are given; it assumes the user has supplied what's needed once an argument is present, and does not re-validate or force a prompt
No — context: fork disables prompting behavior for any skill run as a sub-agent
Yes, but only because argument-hint silently validates the argument against a schema before deciding whether to prompt
questions.explain:
argument-hint is autocomplete guidance shown when a skill is invoked without arguments; once an argument is supplied, the skill proceeds on the assumption the user has provided what's needed. It isn't a schema or a validator, so it doesn't force a prompt regardless of input (ruling out A and D), and context: fork governs execution isolation, not prompting behavior.
Not “No — argument-hint should always prompt regardless of whether arg…” — argument-hint is autocomplete guidance, not a forced prompt, so no prompt appearing when an argument is supplied is expected rather than a bug.
Not “No — context: fork disables prompting behavior for any skill run …” — context: fork controls execution isolation, not whether the skill prompts for input, so it does not explain the missing prompt.
Not “Yes, but only because argument-hint silently validates the argume…” — argument-hint does not validate against any schema. It is only a hint shown when no arguments are given.

questions.q: A developer spends over two hours exploring a large, unfamiliar monorepo — reading 40+ files, tracing call chains, and building a mental model of a thread-safety requirement documented in a file read early in the session. Near the end of the session, they ask Claude to refactor the module for readability. The refactor passes unit tests but breaks a downstream integration test because it violates that early thread-safety requirement — which Claude never cites or references while making the change. What should have been done differently during exploration?
options: Run /compact after every new file is read, aggressively trimming context to make room for new information
Maintain a scratchpad file recording critical constraints, assumptions, and invariants discovered during exploration, so they can be explicitly rechecked before any later implementation step
Restart the session every 90 minutes to avoid context window saturation
Only ever use the Explore subagent for discovery, and always implement in a completely fresh session afterward
questions.explain:
A scratchpad recording constraints and invariants discovered during exploration is what lets a later implementation step recheck against them explicitly, instead of relying on the model to spontaneously recall something read an hour earlier in a long session. Aggressive /compact and periodic restarts both actively discard the very information that needed to be preserved.
Not “Run /compact after every new file is read, aggressively trimming …” — Compacting after every file discards details such as the thread-safety requirement, which is exactly the kind of information that needs preserving.
Not “Restart the session every 90 minutes to avoid context window satura…” — Restarting every 90 minutes throws away what was learned unless it was recorded, so the constraint would be lost as well.
Not “Only ever use the Explore subagent for discovery, and always impl…” — Using Explore for discovery and a fresh session for implementation still loses any constraint that was not written down along the way.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates research on climate-policy evolution to five subagents — recent legislative news, long-form policy documents, emerging green-tech companies, synthesis, and report generation. All five complete without errors. The synthesis subagent's output is coherent, but the final report heavily emphasizes legislative updates and barely mentions green-tech market dynamics, despite the coordinator having requested balanced coverage. Each subagent's individual findings contain relevant material on their assigned topic. Where is the defect most likely located?
options: The green-tech subagent silently failed to execute its task properly
The synthesis subagent's tool access is too narrow to retrieve the green-tech material it needs
The coordinator's decomposition never established weighting or integration instructions, so synthesis had no guidance on how to balance the two domains
The report-generation subagent is intentionally suppressing green-tech findings due to its writing style
questions.explain:
Every subagent executing correctly rules out execution-level defects; the imbalance traces back to the coordinator never giving synthesis any weighting or integration guidance for how to combine the two domains. This is the scenario's signature trap: a "successful" pipeline with a decomposition-level bug.
Not “The green-tech subagent silently failed to execute its task properly” — All five subagents completed without errors and each produced relevant findings on its topic, so nothing indicates the green-tech agent failed.
Not “The synthesis subagent's tool access is too narrow to retrieve the …” — The synthesis agent had the green-tech findings in its input. The imbalance came from missing weighting guidance, not from lack of tool access.
Not “The report-generation subagent is intentionally suppressing green-t…” — Nothing suggests the report generator suppressed green-tech content intentionally. The coordinator never told synthesis how to balance the domains.

questions.q: A web-search subagent completes research on a regulatory topic and returns its findings to the coordinator. The coordinator then delegates a follow-up task to a synthesis subagent. The synthesis subagent immediately asks what "approval timeline" refers to — a term defined only in the earlier search results, which the coordinator has but did not include in the new invocation. Why is this the expected behavior rather than a bug?
options: Subagents automatically inherit all prior coordinator messages and tool outputs, but only if explicitly "enabled" in the invocation — which wasn't done here

Subagents have isolated context by design and do not automatically receive prior conversation history; the coordinator must explicitly pass whatever context a subagent needs into its invocation prompt
The synthesis subagent's context window is smaller than the coordinator's, so large search results are silently truncated before being passed along
Passing context explicitly is optional in principle; the model's training data typically fills in plausible prior search results
questions.explain:
Subagents don't automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history — this is by design, not a defect. Context needed by a subagent must be explicitly included in its invocation prompt, which is exactly what didn't happen here.
Not “Subagents automatically inherit all prior coordinator messages and …” — Subagents have no setting that makes them inherit prior messages. Context must be written into the invocation prompt itself.
Not “The synthesis subagent's context window is smaller than the coordin…” — Nothing in the scenario involves truncation by context size. The synthesis agent simply was never given the earlier results.
Not “Passing context explicitly is optional in principle; the model's tr…” — Training data cannot supply the definition of a term from earlier search results, so context has to be passed explicitly.

questions.q: A coordinator needs to search academic papers, government filings, and corporate financial disclosures on a renewable-energy topic. It currently delegates to one subagent, waits, delegates to a second, waits, then delegates to a third — a fully sequential chain that takes 45 seconds per research cycle. The three lookups don't depend on each other's output. What change reduces elapsed time while keeping the coordinator in control of synthesis?
options: Combine all three into one subagent that internally parallelizes the three lookups itself
Emit all three Task tool calls within a single coordinator turn so the subagents run concurrently
Use Bash to shell out to a script that invokes all three subagents in parallel, bypassing the Task tool
Reduce each subagent's context window so results come back faster
questions.explain:
Emitting multiple Task calls within a single coordinator turn is what runs subagents concurrently. Sequential delegation (the current setup) is what's producing the 45-second elapsed time; combining the three lookups into one subagent or shelling out via Bash both abandon the coordinator's oversight of the delegation itself.
Not “Combine all three into one subagent that internally parallelizes th…” — Merging the three lookups into one subagent that parallelises internally takes delegation out of the coordinator's oversight instead of running the subagents concurrently.
Not “Use Bash to shell out to a script that invokes all three subagent…” — Shelling out through Bash bypasses the Task tool and moves delegation out of the coordinator's control.
Not “Reduce each subagent's context window so results come back faster” — Smaller context windows do not change how delegation is ordered, so the three lookups would still run one after another.

questions.q: A document-analysis subagent queries a restricted research database for licensing information. Every failure — expired license, database outage, malformed input, or a valid search with zero matching records — comes back as {"isError": true, "message": "Request failed"}. The coordinator can't reliably decide whether to retry, reformat the input, escalate for license renewal, or move on with a documented coverage gap. What should the tool result include instead?
options: A generic success/failure boolean, leaving recovery logic entirely to the coordinator's judgment
Structured error context: category (expired/timeout/validation/not-found), whether retrying is worthwhile, what was attempted, and a suggested next step
A confidence score reflecting how sure the subagent is that the call actually failed
A verbose internal log of every retry the subagent already attempted, for the coordinator to replay
questions.explain:
Categorized error context — cause, retryability, what was attempted, and a suggested next step — is what lets the coordinator make an informed recovery decision instead of guessing. A bare boolean or a self-reported confidence score don't distinguish a temporary outage from a permission problem, which is exactly the ambiguity causing unpredictable recovery here.
Not “A generic success/failure boolean, leaving recovery logic entirely …” — A bare success or failure flag cannot distinguish an expired license from an outage or a no-match search, so the coordinator is left guessing.
Not “A confidence score reflecting how sure the subagent is that the cal…” — A confidence score about whether the call failed does not identify the type of failure or whether retrying would help.
Not “A verbose internal log of every retry the subagent already attempte…” — A verbose retry log gives raw material but not a categorised cause or a recommended next step, leaving the coordinator to interpret it.

questions.q: A research coordinator's usual flow is: search → wait → analysis (with search results) → wait → synthesis. On complex topics, the coordinator sometimes needs analysis and synthesis dispatched together right after search results land; on simple topics, synthesis should start the moment analysis returns, without an extra coordinator round-trip. The right next step genuinely depends on what each stage discovers. What orchestration approach fits best?
options: A fixed four-step prompt chain that always runs in the same order, on the theory that predictability beats adaptive logic
A dynamic orchestrator that inspects results after each step and decides which subagents to invoke next based on what it finds
Let each specialist subagent independently decide when to hand its output to the next stage, without the coordinator tracking overall progress
Merge search, analysis, and synthesis into one subagent operating in a single context window
questions.explain:
When the right next step depends on what a stage actually finds, a dynamic orchestrator that inspects results and decides subsequent delegation is the fit — this is the orchestrator-workers pattern. A fixed chain can't adapt when complex topics need a different dispatch shape than simple ones.
Not “A fixed four-step prompt chain that always runs in the same order, …” — A fixed chain cannot adjust to complex topics that need a different dispatch pattern from simple ones, so it ignores the decisions made after each stage.
Not “Let each specialist subagent independently decide when to hand its …” — Without the coordinator tracking overall progress, there is no central point deciding the next step, so coordination and error handling suffer.
Not “Merge search, analysis, and synthesis into one subagent operating i…” — One subagent doing everything gives up specialised delegation and cannot adapt dispatch to what each stage finds.

questions.q: A finance-research system has fetch_market_data (stock prices, trading volumes, market indices) and fetch_economic_indicators (GDP, unemployment, inflation from government sources), described only as "Retrieves market information" and "Retrieves economic information" respectively. Logs show the synthesis subagent frequently calls fetch_market_data for inflation figures and fetch_economic_indicators for stock prices — both tools work correctly when called, they're just being selected for the wrong job. What's the most effective first fix?
options: Add 10 few-shot examples showing correct tool selection for each data type

Rewrite both descriptions with specific input formats, example queries, the exact data types each returns, and explicit boundaries (e.g., "use fetch_market_data only for prices and trading volumes, never macroeconomic aggregates")
Remove one of the two tools and route all lookups through the survivor
Add a keyword-based pre-router that intercepts the request and picks the tool before the model sees it
questions.explain:
Thin, near-identical descriptions ("Retrieves market information" / "Retrieves economic information") give the model no basis for correct selection. Rewriting both with specific inputs, example queries, and explicit boundaries is the first and highest-leverage fix, ahead of few-shot examples or a pre-router.
Not “Add 10 few-shot examples showing correct tool selection for each da…” — A handful of few-shot examples is the next lever only after the thin descriptions have been rewritten, so it comes later.
Not “Remove one of the two tools and route all lookups through the survivor” — Removing a tool takes away a capability the system needs, when both tools work correctly and simply need clearer descriptions.
Not “Add a keyword-based pre-router that intercepts the request and pick…” — A keyword pre-router adds brittle external logic when the cheaper first fix is to give the tools specific descriptions.

questions.q: A draft report synthesized from three subagents' findings states a renewable-energy adoption statistic with no source citation, even though the search subagent originally found this figure in a credible government report and passed it along with a source reference. The synthesis subagent had both the number and the source in its input; the citation was simply dropped during synthesis. What should have been required from the start to prevent this?
options: A confidence score on each claim, so synthesis can prioritize high-confidence findings
Structured claim-source mappings — each assertion explicitly linked to its source document, excerpt, date, and methodology — that synthesis is required to preserve rather than compress away
A checklist forcing the synthesis subagent to manually copy-paste every source reference verbatim into the output
A separate "sources" file kept entirely outside the synthesis subagent's input context
questions.explain:
Structured claim-source mappings — claim, excerpt, source, date, methodology — carried through as a required part of the handoff are what prevent provenance from being silently dropped during synthesis. A confidence score doesn't address citation loss, and a checklist or externally-stored sources file both rely on a manual step that's easy to skip under exactly the conditions that caused the original loss.
Not “A confidence score on each claim, so synthesis can prioritize high-…” — A confidence score does not preserve the citation. Synthesis dropped the source, and a score says nothing about where the figure came from.
Not “A checklist forcing the synthesis subagent to manually copy-paste e…” — A copy-paste checklist relies on a manual step that is easy to skip, which is how the citation was lost in the first place.
Not “A separate "sources" file kept entirely outside the synthesis subag…” — Keeping sources out of the synthesis agent's input removes the very information it would need to attach the citation to each claim.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates in parallel to three subagents: clinical-trial outcomes, healthcare policy documents, and emerging medical technologies. Trials and policy both return successfully. The technology subagent errors out because a source is temporarily unreachable. A report can still be produced, just with a coverage gap on emerging technologies. What should the coordinator do?
options: Escalate the whole pipeline to a human, since any subagent failure should halt the process regardless of how much useful work the others completed
Produce the partial report from the two completed subagents, clearly annotating the coverage gap and why it exists, and let the reader judge whether that gap matters for their purposes
Retry the failed subagent indefinitely and block the report until it eventually succeeds
Discard the two successful results too, since the three-subagent pipeline was defined as all-or-nothing
questions.explain:
A partial, clearly-annotated report lets the reader judge whether the coverage gap matters for their purposes, while still delivering the value already produced by the two subagents that succeeded. Escalating over one failed subagent, retrying indefinitely, or discarding good work all destroy value the pipeline has already legitimately produced.
Not “Escalate the whole pipeline to a human, since any subagent failure …” — Halting the entire pipeline over one failed subagent discards the useful work from the two that succeeded.
Not “Retry the failed subagent indefinitely and block the report until i…” — Retrying forever and blocking the report holds everything up on a source that may stay unreachable, so the reader gets nothing.
Not “Discard the two successful results too, since the three-subagent pi…” — Throwing away the two successful results wastes valid work, and nothing requires the pipeline to be all-or-nothing.

questions.q: A multi-turn synthesis is tracking housing-policy changes across a decade — early turns cover 2015–2018 findings, later turns add 2019–2024. By turn 5, the synthesis subagent starts referencing "typical housing-policy patterns" in vague generalities instead of the specific policy names, agencies, and dates it correctly cited in turn 2. The coordinator's messages keep growing, but the output keeps getting vaguer. What's the most direct fix?
options: Restart the research from scratch with no prior context, since this kind of degradation is unavoidable in long sessions

Maintain a persistent findings-summary artifact (key facts, dates, policy names, sources) that the coordinator re-injects into every synthesis turn, countering attention loss on details buried in the middle of a growing context
Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to generate detailed responses
Swap in a larger model mid-session to regain synthesis quality
questions.explain:
A persistent findings-summary artifact, re-injected into every synthesis turn, is the direct countermeasure to specific facts getting buried and generalized away as a long multi-turn session grows — the classic "lost in the middle" pattern. Restarting, raising max_tokens, or swapping models don't address why the earlier, more specific findings stopped being referenced.
Not “Restart the research from scratch with no prior context, since this…” — Restarting from scratch throws away all gathered findings, and the degradation is avoidable by re-injecting the key facts into each turn.
Not “Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to generate detailed …” — max_tokens limits response length. It does nothing to bring back details that have become buried in a growing context.
Not “Swap in a larger model mid-session to regain synthesis quality” — A larger model does not address why earlier specifics stopped being referenced, since the facts are still buried in the long context.

questions.q: A developer asks Claude to "find all places where the request handler deserializes payloads without a null check" while investigating intermittent null-pointer exceptions. Claude runs Grep, finds 14 matching files, reads three of them, and concludes with a vague "most callers look safe." Asked for a specific prioritized list of entry points to review, Claude admits it only read a small fraction of the 14 matches. What's the most direct fix for the next investigation?
options: Increase the context window so Claude can read all 14 files in one pass
Maintain a scratchpad file recording each candidate file's path, line number, and null-check status as it's checked, before synthesizing a final answer
Replace Grep with a more elaborate Bash find pipeline to pre-filter matches
Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to "be thorough" when reviewing security-sensitive code
questions.explain:
A scratchpad tracking each candidate's path, line number, and status as it's actually checked gives Claude a persistent record to synthesize from, instead of drawing a conclusion from a small, arbitrary subset of the 14 matches. A bigger context window doesn't force the remaining 11 files to actually get checked, and "be thorough" is a probabilistic instruction, not a structural fix.
Not “Increase the context window so Claude can read all 14 files in one …” — A bigger window lets more fit in but does not force Claude to actually check each of the 14 files, so a partial review could recur.
Not “Replace Grep with a more elaborate Bash find pipeline to pre-fi…” — A more elaborate Bash find pipeline filters differently but does not record which candidates were examined or what was found.
Not “Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to "be thorough" whe…” — Telling Claude to be thorough is a probabilistic instruction. It does not create a record of each file's status to synthesise from.

questions.q: An MCP server code_analyzer exposes find_pattern (pattern/regex matching over code) and trace_dataflow (semantic, cross-function-boundary analysis that can follow unsanitized input to a security-critical sink). trace_dataflow is strictly more capable for this class of investigation, but logs show Claude consistently reaches for find_pattern instead, even on tasks that clearly call for cross-boundary tracing. What's the most likely cause?
options: The built-in Grep tool has higher precedence than any MCP tool and is preferred by default
trace_dataflow's description doesn't clearly explain its semantic, cross-boundary capability or when it should be chosen over simple pattern matching
The MCP server needs to be reconfigured at the network level to expose trace_dataflow with higher priority
Claude prefers MCP tools over built-ins by default, so some other, unrelated setting must be suppressing that preference here
questions.explain:
Tool selection is driven primarily by description quality; a thin or vague description for the more capable tool loses to a familiar, simpler alternative by default. Sharpening trace_dataflow's description to spell out its semantic, cross-boundary capability — and when that capability actually matters — is the direct fix, well ahead of anything at the network or precedence level.
Not “The built-in Grep tool has higher precedence than any MCP tool an…” — Built-in Grep does not have fixed precedence over MCP tools. A weak description is what makes the familiar alternative win.
Not “The MCP server needs to be reconfigured at the network level to exp…” — Network configuration would not affect which tool Claude prefers, as the tool is exposed and callable but just not chosen.
Not “Claude prefers MCP tools over built-ins by default, so some other, …” — Claude does not generally prefer MCP tools over built-ins, so this assumes a default that does not exist and leaves the thin description unaddressed.

questions.q: A developer wants to compare one function's signature across three branches (main, develop, staging) — just the definition line and its parameter list in each. What's the most efficient combination of built-in tools?
options: Use Bash to run git diff across the branches and parse the raw output
Use Grep to locate the function's definition line in each branch, then Read only the small region around each match
Use Glob to enumerate every source file first, then Read each one looking for the signature
Use Read on the entire repository per branch, then search the combined content manually
questions.explain:
Grep is the right tool for finding a pattern (the function definition) inside file contents, and Read is then used narrowly on just the matched region. Glob matches file paths, not contents, and reading entire branches wastes context on code that isn't relevant to the comparison.
Not “Use Bash to run git diff across the branches and parse the raw …” — git diff output is a different comparison, and parsing raw output is clumsy for just one function's signature across three branches.
Not “Use Glob to enumerate every source file first, then Read each o…” — Glob matches file paths, not contents, so it cannot find a signature, and reading every file wastes effort.
Not “Use Read on the entire repository per branch, then search the com…” — Reading the entire repository per branch floods the context with code irrelevant to a single signature comparison.

questions.q: An Edit call's anchor text matches three times in the target file: once in a comment, once in a docstring, and once in the actual executable line the developer wants changed. The call fails because the anchor isn't unique. What's the reliable next step?
options: Retry Edit with a longer anchor string that includes more surrounding context, hoping it becomes unique
Use Read to load the full file, manually identify the correct occurrence, then use Write to save the corrected full-file version
Use Bash grep -n to get the line number, then build a new Edit call anchored on that line number
Tell the user ambiguous anchors are a hard limitation and the edit must be done manually
questions.explain:
When an Edit anchor isn't unique, the documented fallback is Read to load the whole file, manually identify the correct occurrence, then Write the corrected full-file version. A longer anchor might still collide, and constructing an Edit around a bare line number isn't how the tool matches text.
Not “Retry Edit with a longer anchor string that includes more surroun…” — A longer anchor might still match more than once, so it is not reliable, whereas rewriting the full file avoids the ambiguity completely.
Not “Use Bash grep -n to get the line number, then build a new Edit …” — Edit matches text, not line numbers, so anchoring it on a line number is not how the tool works.
Not “Tell the user ambiguous anchors are a hard limitation and the edit …” — Ambiguous anchors are not a hard limit, since reading the file and writing the corrected version works.

questions.q: A custom MCP server queries a proprietary internal database for team-wide metrics. It needs credentials that must never be committed to git, and the server configuration itself must be shared across every developer's checkout. Where should this be configured, and how should the credential be referenced?
options: In ~/.claude.json, with the credential hardcoded, distributed manually to each teammate
In .mcp.json, referencing ${DATABASE_API_KEY} for environment-variable expansion, with each developer setting that variable locally
In CLAUDE.md, inside a fenced code block, with a note asking developers not to commit it
In a root-level .env file, referenced from .mcp.json by its literal filename
questions.explain:
Project-scoped .mcp.json, committed to version control, with ${DATABASE_API_KEY} expanded from each developer's own environment, is exactly the pattern that keeps the config shared while keeping the secret itself out of git. ~/.claude.json isn't shared across the team by design.
Not “In ~/.claude.json, with the credential hardcoded, distributed man…” — ~/.claude.json is personal and not shared by design, and hardcoding the credential puts the secret in a file passed around by hand.
Not “In CLAUDE.md, inside a fenced code block, with a note asking deve…” — CLAUDE.md is committed to the repo, so the credential would end up in git, and asking people not to commit it is unenforceable.
Not “In a root-level .env file, referenced from .mcp.json by its lit…” — A .env file referenced by its literal filename is not how .mcp.json picks up credentials. It expands variables from the environment.

questions.q: A developer wants to try out a prototype MCP server for dependency-graph analysis that no one else on the team needs yet, and that might be misconfigured and break things while they experiment. Where should this go so it doesn't affect teammates or clutter shared config?
options: In .mcp.json at the repo root, flagged with an "experimental": true field
In ~/.claude.json on their own machine
In a new .claude/experimental-mcp.json file in the project
In a .mcp-local file added to .gitignore
questions.explain:
~/.claude.json is the user-scoped location intended for exactly this: a personal, experimental server that shouldn't be pushed into the shared project configuration or risk breaking anything for teammates.
Not “In .mcp.json at the repo root, flagged with an `"experimental": t…” — A flag inside .mcp.json does not keep the server out of the shared file, so teammates would still receive the prototype.
Not “In a new .claude/experimental-mcp.json file in the project” — A new file in the project is not a recognised configuration location for MCP servers, and it would sit in the shared project.
Not “In a .mcp-local file added to .gitignore” — A .mcp-local file is not a location Claude Code reads for server configuration, so the server would not be registered.

questions.q: After three hours exploring a monorepo's service-to-service communication, Claude has answered several detailed questions correctly, citing specific classes. On the next question — about the same system — Claude says it "doesn't have enough context to be specific." Asked to recall a class name it named accurately 15 minutes earlier, it now proposes a slightly different, incorrect name. What's happening, and what's the most direct fix?
options: The context window is full; restart the session

The agent's grip on earlier specifics is degrading as the conversation grows; maintain a scratchpad file recording key class names, interface boundaries, and dependency relationships, and reference it in later prompts
The developer's questions have become too vague; ask more specific, narrowly-scoped questions instead
Reduce max_tokens so responses stay short enough to avoid straining context
questions.explain:
This is context degradation over a long session — earlier specifics get lost even though the conversation is still "about" the same system. A scratchpad recording key class names and relationships, referenced in later prompts, is the direct mitigation. Restarting throws away three hours of legitimate exploration.
Not “The context window is full; restart the session” — Restarting throws away three hours of exploration, and the issue is gradual loss of specifics, not a simple full-window condition.
Not “The developer's questions have become too vague; ask more specific,…” — The questions are fine. The agent is losing specifics it already held, so rephrasing them does not restore the details.
