Not “Reduce max_tokens so responses stay short enough to avoid straini…” — max_tokens caps response length and does nothing to preserve earlier class names across a long session.

questions.q: A developer unfamiliar with a codebase wants to find where HTTP request validation happens before requests reach business logic, without reading every file upfront. What's the recommended exploration order?
options: Use Read on every file under /handlers first, to understand overall structure
Use Grep for validation-related terms ("validate", "schema", "middleware") to find candidate files, then use Read on just those matches, following imports to trace the flow from entry points
Use Bash find to list files, pipe the output somewhere, and ask Claude to infer the pattern from the file list alone
Use Glob for **/*.ts, then Read every result and ask Claude to identify validation logic after the fact
questions.explain:
Search first, read second: Grep for validation-related terms surfaces candidate files, then Read on just those matches (following imports from there) builds understanding incrementally. Reading everything upfront front-loads irrelevant content before knowing what actually matters.
Not “Use Read on every file under /handlers first, to understand ove…” — Reading every handler file first is slow and fills the context with code unrelated to validation before knowing what matters.
Not “Use Bash find to list files, pipe the output somewhere, and ask C…” — Inferring a pattern from a file list alone gives no information about what the files contain, so it cannot locate validation logic.
Not “Use Glob for **/*.ts, then Read every result and ask Claude t…” — Reading every file after listing them front-loads irrelevant content and defeats targeted exploration.

questions.q: A team's custom MCP server for repo analysis is configured in .mcp.json with ${GIT_API_TOKEN} for credential expansion. A teammate launches Claude Code and the server fails to initialize with an error that the environment variable isn't set — even though they've added export GIT_API_TOKEN=... to their ~/.bashrc. What's actually going on, and what's the fix?
options: Credentials referenced via environment-variable expansion only work from ~/.claude.json, not .mcp.json

A variable set in ~/.bashrc only applies to shells that source that file when they start; if Claude Code was launched from a shell or process that never sourced it, the variable simply isn't in its environment — export it in the current terminal session (or set it at the OS/session level) before launching Claude Code
The syntax is wrong; it must be ${GIT_API_TOKEN:-default}, since bare ${VAR} isn't supported
Environment-variable expansion isn't supported in .mcp.json at all; the token must be hardcoded or read from a separate .env file
questions.explain:
A variable exported only in ~/.bashrc is available to shells that source that file at startup — it doesn't automatically propagate to every process on the machine. If Claude Code was launched from a context that never sourced .bashrc, the variable simply isn't present in its environment. The fix is ensuring the variable is actually set in the shell/session Claude Code is launched from — this is standard environment-variable scoping, not an .mcp.json syntax or location problem.
Not “Credentials referenced via environment-variable expansion only work…” — Credential expansion works in .mcp.json. The issue lies in where the variable exists, not in which file refers to it.
Not “The syntax is wrong; it must be ${GIT_API_TOKEN:-default}, since …” — Bare ${VAR} is supported, so a default-value syntax is not required, and the error says the variable is unset.
Not “Environment-variable expansion isn't supported in .mcp.json at al…” — Environment-variable expansion is supported in .mcp.json, and it is the right way to keep tokens out of version control.

questions.q: A team wants an exploration phase (read-only: Read, Grep, Bash restricted to read-only commands) to hand off to a separate modification phase (Read, Write, Edit) once a refactor target is identified — without maintaining two entirely disconnected agents. What's the best way to enforce this tool scoping?
options: Configure allowedTools at each agent/role definition so exploration and modification each only ever have access to the tools appropriate for that phase
Build two fully separate agent definitions that share no context whatsoever between phases
Use a single agent and rely on prompt instructions telling it which tools to avoid during the exploration phase
Use hooks to dynamically intercept and block any tool call not on the current phase's approved list
questions.explain:
allowedTools scoped at the agent/role definition is exactly the mechanism for restricting which tools are available during which phase, without needing two fully disconnected agents or relying on prompt instructions alone to enforce what should be a hard boundary.
Not “Build two fully separate agent definitions that share no context wh…” — Two fully separate agent definitions that share no context make the handoff between phases hard, which is what the team wants to avoid.
Not “Use a single agent and rely on prompt instructions telling it which…” — Prompt instructions about which tools to avoid are followed probabilistically, so they cannot enforce a firm read-only boundary.
Not “Use hooks to dynamically intercept and block any tool call not on t…” — Hooks can block calls but add complexity to track phases dynamically, whereas scoping allowedTools per role defines the boundary directly.

questions.q: A CI pipeline reuses a single Claude Code session across a queue of 6–8 PRs to amortize session startup overhead. By the third PR, review comments start referencing prior PRs ("similar to the previous refactoring"); by the seventh, findings are generic and don't address the actual diff in front of it. Why, and what's the fix?
options: The session's context window is exhausted; raise max_tokens to give each invocation more room
The session is carrying forward reasoning and context from earlier PRs, biasing later reviews toward prior patterns; use a fresh Claude Code session per PR instead
The CI runner is incorrectly caching findings between invocations; clear the runner's cache
Run all PR reviews simultaneously in parallel instead of sequentially, to avoid context accumulation
questions.explain:
Reusing one session across multiple PRs lets earlier reasoning and context bleed into later reviews, producing generic, prior-PR-flavored comments instead of a focused read of the current diff. A fresh session per PR removes that contamination. Raising max_tokens doesn't address contaminated context, and parallelizing sidesteps the question of what's actually wrong with the sequential design rather than fixing it.
Not “The session's context window is exhausted; raise max_tokens to gi…” — max_tokens limits response length. It does not clear earlier PRs' reasoning from the session, which is what contaminates later reviews.
Not “The CI runner is incorrectly caching findings between invocations; …” — Nothing indicates the runner caches findings. The earlier PRs' context sits in the long-lived session itself.
Not “Run all PR reviews simultaneously in parallel instead of sequential…” — Running reviews in parallel in the same shared session would not remove contamination, and it avoids rather than fixes the shared-context problem.

questions.q: A PostToolUse hook with matcher: "Bash|Read|Edit" normalizes tool responses into a consistent JSON structure to make review output more uniform. In CI, the same hook also fires on an unrelated test-execution Bash step that emits raw plain-text test output, and normalizing that output breaks the downstream test-result parser, which now fails the build. What's the most precise fix?
options: Remove the hook entirely and give up on normalizing tool responses in CI
Narrow the hook's matcher (or add a condition) so it only fires on review-related tool invocations, not on the unrelated test-execution step
Move the hook from PostToolUse to PreToolUse, since that runs earlier and can skip non-review steps
Disable Bash tool access for the entire CI review run and use only Read and Edit
questions.explain:
The hook's logic is sound; its scope is too broad. Narrowing the matcher (or adding a condition) so it only fires on review-related tool calls — not on an unrelated test-execution step — fixes the interference without giving up normalization altogether or misdiagnosing the fix as a timing change.
Not “Remove the hook entirely and give up on normalizing tool responses …” — Removing the hook gives up normalisation that works for review output, when the only problem is its overly broad scope.
Not “Move the hook from PostToolUse to PreToolUse, since that runs e…” — Moving to PreToolUse changes timing but does not narrow which tool calls the hook affects, so it would still fire on the test step.
Not “Disable Bash tool access for the entire CI review run and use onl…” — Disabling Bash for the whole review run removes a needed tool and does not fix the hook's scope.

questions.q: A CI review prompt spells out separate false-positive-reduction criteria for nine finding categories (security, performance, coverage, etc.), totaling roughly 280 tokens of criteria alone. Traces show the model applies these criteria inconsistently and sometimes seems to forget earlier categories' rules by the time it reaches later files in the same pass. What's the underlying issue?
options: The criteria are too strict; loosen them so the reviewer becomes more confident overall

Packing many fine-grained, per-category rules into a single pass causes attention dilution; split the review into per-category (or per-file) passes, or move some of the criteria into a deterministic post-generation validation layer
Add 5–8 few-shot examples per category showing correct criterion application
Set temperature: 0 to force strictly rule-following, deterministic behavior regardless of prompt length
questions.explain:
Nine categories' worth of fine-grained criteria packed into a single pass is a recipe for attention dilution — the model can't reliably hold and apply that many rules while also reading code. Splitting into per-category (or per-file) passes, or moving some of the criteria into a deterministic post-generation validation step, addresses the structural cause. More examples or forcing temperature: 0 don't resolve rules competing for the same attention budget.
Not “The criteria are too strict; loosen them so the reviewer becomes mo…” — Looser criteria would raise false positives and do nothing about the model dropping earlier rules when it handles many of them in one pass.
Not “Add 5–8 few-shot examples per category showing correct criterion ap…” — Adding more examples per category lengthens the prompt further, increasing the attention load rather than reducing it.
Not “Set temperature: 0 to force strictly rule-following, deterministi…” — Temperature zero does not give the model more attention capacity, so rules would still compete for it across a long prompt.

questions.q: A team runs a blocking pre-merge review with an SLA of under 8 minutes, and a separate nightly technical-debt scan with no time constraint. They want to move workloads to the Message Batches API for the 50% cost discount. Which is the correct call?
options: Batch both; the cost savings are worth accepting whatever latency impact results

Batch only the nightly scan; moving the pre-merge check to the Batches API would only make sense if the team is willing to accept processing delays of up to 24 hours on merge decisions, which conflicts with the stated SLA
Batch the pre-merge check too — the Batches API typically finishes within about 2 hours, which is fine for most teams' merge cadence
Keep both synchronous; the Batches API isn't appropriate for any CI-adjacent workflow
questions.explain:
The Message Batches API has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours; that's fundamentally incompatible with an under-8-minute blocking pre-merge check, but is a good fit for the latency-tolerant nightly scan. Assuming a typical 2-hour turnaround treats an unbounded window as if it were a guarantee, which it isn't.
Not “Batch both; the cost savings are worth accepting whatever latency i…” — Batching the blocking pre-merge check would put merge decisions behind a processing window of up to 24 hours, breaking the under-8-minute requirement.
Not “Batch the pre-merge check too — the Batches API typically finishes …” — Batch has no latency guarantee. A typical turnaround is not a promise, so a blocking check cannot rely on it.
Not “Keep both synchronous; the Batches API isn't appropriate for any CI…” — The nightly scan has no time constraint and suits batch well, so keeping everything synchronous gives up an easy 50% saving.

questions.q: A CI reviewer is configured to emit --output-format json with a --json-schema, and a downstream bot parses that JSON to post PR comments. The bot has recently started rejecting otherwise-valid runs because a finding's text field contains a literal { or } (e.g., "O{n} complexity" or "refactor: {old} → {new}"), which trips up a naive bracket-counting step the bot added as an extra sanity check before parsing. What's the most robust fix?
options: Have the bot search for the first [ in the raw response and parse only from there onward
Add a prompt instruction: "output JSON only, no prose before or after"

Remove the bot's ad hoc bracket-sanity-check step and parse directly against the enforced --json-schema, since schema-enforced output is already structurally reliable and the extra heuristic is what's actually misfiring on legitimate content
Have the bot trigger a second review run with a different prompt whenever the first one fails to parse
questions.explain:
--output-format json with --json-schema already produces structurally enforced, schema-valid JSON; the bracket-counting sanity check the bot added on top is a redundant heuristic that misfires on legitimate finding text containing {/}. Removing that extra, unnecessary check and parsing directly against the enforced schema is more robust than patching around it with string-search heuristics or hoping a prompt instruction prevents {/} from ever appearing in prose.
Not “Have the bot search for the first [ in the raw response and parse…” — Patching around a redundant heuristic by searching for the first [ is brittle, and the schema-enforced output does not need such parsing tricks.
Not “Add a prompt instruction: "output JSON only, no prose before or after"” — The output is already schema-enforced, so more prompting is unnecessary, and instructions cannot control whether finding text contains braces.
Not “Have the bot trigger a second review run with a different prompt wh…” — A second review run does nothing about the bot's faulty bracket check, which would reject the same valid output again.

questions.q: A team wants to guarantee that review never runs on a PR lacking a linked issue-tracker ticket — unlinked PRs currently produce findings that just get ignored downstream anyway. The review prompt already says "never review PRs without a linked ticket," but reviews keep running regardless, since prompt instructions are followed probabilistically. What's the most deterministic enforcement point?
options: Strengthen the prompt further: "CRITICAL: you MUST refuse to review PRs without a confirmed linked ticket. Non-negotiable."
Add a PreToolUse hook that checks the ticket-link prerequisite via the issue tracker's API and blocks the review-related tool call outright if the check fails
Build a custom /review skill that checks for a linked ticket as a documented step in its instructions before invoking the reviewer
Let review run as normal, then filter out and discard any findings after the fact if the PR turns out to lack a linked ticket
questions.explain:
A non-negotiable prerequisite needs enforcement outside the model's voluntary compliance. A PreToolUse hook that checks the ticket-link prerequisite and blocks the review tool call deterministically is the fix; a stronger prompt, a skill that merely documents the check as a step, or post-hoc filtering all still depend on the model behaving correctly, which has already been shown to fail.
Not “Strengthen the prompt further: "CRITICAL: you MUST refuse to review…” — Stronger wording is still followed probabilistically, and the model has already been shown to ignore the existing instruction.
Not “Build a custom /review skill that checks for a linked ticket as a…” — A skill that lists the check as a step still relies on the model following it, so it is not enforced.
Not “Let review run as normal, then filter out and discard any findings …” — Filtering findings after the review has run wastes the review work and does not prevent the review from running.

questions.q: A team splits large PR reviews into (1) per-file local-analysis passes and (2) a cross-file integration pass for API-contract and shared-type issues — but both stages currently run as two prompts inside one long-lived session. In practice, the integration pass re-flags issues the per-file pass already caught, and by the time the integration prompt runs, the accumulated session context has grown large enough that its findings get noticeably less precise. What's the best architectural fix?
options: Keep both stages in the same session, separated by a clear divider comment, and instruct the model not to repeat findings from the prior stage
Run each stage as a separate -p CLI invocation with fresh context, passing the per-file findings into the integration invocation's input so it can focus only on genuinely new cross-file issues
Merge both stages into one comprehensive prompt that analyzes every file at once for full consistency
Run the per-file passes in parallel, but still run the integration pass afterward inside the same accumulated session
questions.explain:
Running each stage as its own fresh -p invocation avoids both the session-bloat precision loss and the re-flagging problem, as long as the per-file findings are explicitly passed into the integration invocation so it knows what's already been caught and can focus on genuinely new cross-file issues. Keeping both stages in one long session preserves the very context accumulation causing the precision loss.
Not “Keep both stages in the same session, separated by a clear divider …” — A divider comment and an instruction not to repeat findings leave both stages in one growing session, so the precision loss from accumulated context remains.
Not “Merge both stages into one comprehensive prompt that analyzes every…” — One prompt covering every file at once recreates the attention dilution that splitting into per-file and cross-file passes was meant to solve.
Not “Run the per-file passes in parallel, but still run the integration …” — Parallel per-file passes help, but running integration in the same accumulated session keeps the context bloat and the repeated findings.

questions.q: A reviewer keeps flagging functions as "missing error handling" even when a try/catch is clearly present. The instruction "flag only critical cases where error handling is missing" hasn't helped, and adding 4–5 illustrative good/bad examples hasn't moved the false-positive rate either. What additional specificity is actually needed?
options: Increase the example count from 4–5 to 15+, covering more edge cases
Switch to a larger, more capable model

Replace the vague instruction with an explicit, codebase-specific rule — e.g., "flag only when function X is called outside a try/catch, and the uncaught exception types are Y or Z, which can cause data loss or DB inconsistency"
Disable the "missing error handling" category entirely until a dedicated, separately-trained classifier can be built for it
questions.explain:
"Flag only critical cases" is still a subjective judgment call; an explicit, codebase-specific rule (naming the function, the exception types, and the concrete consequence that matters) removes the ambiguity that examples alone hadn't resolved. More examples without a sharper rule doesn't change the boundary itself.
Not “Increase the example count from 4–5 to 15+, covering more edge cases” — More examples without a sharper rule do not change the vague boundary, and a handful of examples has not moved the false-positive rate already.
Not “Switch to a larger, more capable model” — A more capable model would still be guessing at an undefined threshold, so false positives stay unless the criterion itself is specific.
Not “Disable the "missing error handling" category entirely until a dedi…” — Disabling the category until a separate classifier exists gives up the finding entirely, when a clearer rule would fix the ambiguity.

questions.q: A CI-facing project CLAUDE.md has grown past 650 lines: API design conventions, a deployment-readiness checklist, test-writing standards, migration guidelines, and detailed false-positive-reduction criteria for 15+ finding categories, all loaded on every single invocation regardless of what's actually being reviewed. Reviews are now missing context from the actual diff and producing vaguer findings, and logs show a large share of the context budget going to configuration rather than the code under review. What's the most effective fix?
options: Split CLAUDE.md into several files connected with @path imports, so the content is easier for humans to navigate
Move file-type- or path-specific guidance (e.g., migration rules scoped to paths: ["**/migrations/*"]) into .claude/rules/, and keep only genuinely universal guidance in CLAUDE.md
Cut CLAUDE.md down to under 100 lines of high-level guidance and rely on the model's general training knowledge for the rest
Build a custom /review skill that dynamically selects which subset of guidance to load based on which files changed in the PR
questions.explain:
Moving path- or category-specific guidance into .claude/rules/ with scoped frontmatter means it only loads for matching files, freeing up context budget for the actual diff being reviewed.
Not “Split CLAUDE.md into several files connected with @path imports…” — @path imports organise the content for people but are still expanded into context, so the context budget problem remains.
Not “Cut CLAUDE.md down to under 100 lines of high-level guidance and …” — Cutting to under 100 lines throws away guidance the team needs and relies on general knowledge instead of project-specific rules.
Not “Build a custom /review skill that dynamically selects which subse…” — A custom skill that selects guidance adds machinery and relies on invocation, when path-scoped rules already load only for matching files.

questions.q: A receipt pipeline adds OCR to pull text from vendor logos on scanned images. The model now confidently fills the vendor field with plausible-sounding names that don't appear anywhere in the OCR text, the original image, or the email body — but schema validation passes, since vendor is syntactically a valid string. These hallucinated vendor names carry high confidence scores (0.92) and bypass human review entirely, surfacing only weeks later during downstream reconciliation. What should be added to the schema first to catch this?
options: A required ocr_confidence field, so low-OCR-quality documents can be skipped

A source_location field (e.g., "header", "footer", "email_body", "ocr_image") tracking where each extracted value came from, enabling a validation step that checks the value actually appears in the identified location
An is_hallucinated boolean that the model self-reports
A higher max_tokens budget, giving the model more room to "think" before extracting
questions.explain:
Schema validity guarantees the JSON is well-formed, not that the value is grounded in the source. A source_location field lets downstream validation check that an extracted value actually appears where it claims to have come from, which is what catches a fabricated-but-plausible vendor name that a confidence score alone missed.
Not “A required ocr_confidence field, so low-OCR-quality documents can…” — OCR confidence says how readable the image is, but does not check whether the vendor name appears anywhere in the source.
Not “An is_hallucinated boolean that the model self-reports” — A self-reported hallucination flag relies on the same model that invented the value, which is exactly what cannot be trusted.
Not “A higher max_tokens budget, giving the model more room to "think"…” — More max_tokens gives room for output, not grounding, so the model could still produce a plausible invented vendor.

questions.q: A pipeline has extract_receipt, extract_invoice, and extract_contract, each with its own schema, and uses tool_choice: "any" so a call is always guaranteed. A borderline document — a receipt-like form that also includes itemized line items — keeps getting routed to extract_invoice, whose required fields (like PO_number) don't exist on the source, so the model fabricates them. Retrying with the same tool_choice: "any" setting produces the same misrouted result again. What's the root issue and the most direct fix?
options: Add 2–3 few-shot examples distinguishing a borderline receipt from an invoice, then retry
Switch to tool_choice: "auto" so the model has the option to fall back to a plain-text response instead of a tool call

tool_choice: "any" only guarantees *a* call, not the *right* one; add a validation step that detects field-presence mismatches against the chosen schema, returns a structured error naming the better-fitting schema, and lets the model retry against that feedback
Drop the contract schema — most real documents are receipts or invoices anyway, and fewer options should reduce misrouting
questions.explain:
tool_choice: "any" guarantees a tool call happens, but not that it's the *right* one; that requires a separate validation-retry loop that detects a field-presence mismatch, names the better-fitting schema in a structured error, and lets the model retry against that specific feedback. Few-shot examples may help marginally but don't replace direct error feedback on the actual mismatch.
Not “Add 2–3 few-shot examples distinguishing a borderline receipt from …” — A few examples may help at the margin, but they do not provide direct feedback on the specific field mismatch that causes fabrication.
Not “Switch to tool_choice: "auto" so the model has the option to fall…” — "auto" would allow plain-text responses and no extraction, giving up the guarantee while not fixing the misrouting.
Not “Drop the contract schema — most real documents are receipts or invo…” — Dropping the contract schema removes a document type the pipeline needs and would not stop receipt-like forms being sent to the invoice tool.

questions.q: A pipeline routes extractions below 0.70 overall confidence to human review and auto-approves the rest. After 1,000 documents, fabricated vendor names almost never get caught by review — they only surface weeks later downstream — while extractions that land at 0.68–0.72 confidence (right at the boundary) turn out to be correct almost every time they're checked. What's actually wrong with the routing, and what closes the gap?
options: The threshold is simply too high; drop it to 0.50 so more extractions get reviewed

Confidence is poorly calibrated specifically for fabrication — the model can be very confident about an invented value; add stratified random sampling of a small percentage of *high*-confidence extractions specifically to surface the failure patterns confidence scoring can't see
Field-level confidence is too fine-grained; collapse everything into one binary approve/review decision
Switch from overall confidence to the minimum field-level confidence as the routing signal instead
questions.explain:
Confidence scores are a poor signal specifically for fabrication, since a model can be highly confident about an invented value. Stratified random sampling of a slice of high-confidence extractions is designed to surface exactly the failure patterns a pure confidence threshold structurally cannot catch. Lowering the threshold doesn't target this failure mode any more precisely.
Not “The threshold is simply too high; drop it to 0.50 so more extractio…” — Lowering the threshold sends more items to review but does not target fabricated values that carry high confidence and would still pass.
Not “Field-level confidence is too fine-grained; collapse everything int…” — Collapsing to one binary decision discards information and does not help detect fabricated values that look confident.
Not “Switch from overall confidence to the minimum field-level confidenc…” — Minimum field confidence still relies on the model's confidence, which is unreliable on invented values, so fabrications would still pass.

questions.q: An amount field keeps extracting as the string "1234 dollars" instead of the required numeric type. A retry loop feeds back the original document, the failed output, and the exact validation error each time, but four consecutive retries reproduce the identical mistake. What should happen next, and why is a fifth retry not the answer?
options: Retry a fifth time with a larger max_tokens budget, in case the model needs more room to reason through the fix

Recognize this as a schema-design problem, not a retry problem: accept amount as a string, add a deterministic post-processing step to parse "1234 dollars" into 1234, and move that specific validation out of the pre-approval retry loop entirely
The tokenizer is likely confusing the word "dollars" with the number; rephrase the validation error using only numerals and currency symbols
Persist through up to 10 retries — enough repetition eventually corrects this class of error
questions.explain:
Four identical retries hitting the same wall is a sign the problem is the schema, not the prompt: accept the value as a string and parse it deterministically afterward, moving that check out of the pre-approval retry loop entirely. Persisting with more retries repeats an approach already shown not to work.
Not “Retry a fifth time with a larger max_tokens budget, in case the m…” — max_tokens does not change how the model handles a type mismatch, and four identical retries show more of the same will not work.
Not “The tokenizer is likely confusing the word "dollars" with the numbe…” — The tokenizer is not the issue, and rewording the error message with numerals leaves the underlying schema design problem in place.
Not “Persist through up to 10 retries — enough repetition eventually cor…” — Ten retries repeat an approach that has already failed four times with the same result, so persistence will not fix it.

questions.q: payment_method was originally required, and extraction never failed the schema — but downstream audits found it was frequently fabricated (e.g., "Paid by credit card" invented for documents that never mention payment method at all). Making the field nullable stopped the fabrication, but now roughly 5% of receipts extract with payment_method: null — and some of those actually do state "Paid by credit card" clearly, which the model simply missed. What schema-design principle addresses both problems at once?
options: Revert to required and rely on better prompting to make extraction more reliable
Add a payment_method_confidence field so low-confidence nulls can be distinguished from high-confidence ones

Keep the field optional, but add a source_location (or equivalent evidence field) so "genuinely absent from the source" can be distinguished from "present in source but missed by the model" — the latter is a prompt/extraction bug worth fixing, the former isn't
Default to the string "unknown" instead of null, so the field is always populated
questions.explain:
Making the field optional stops fabrication, but conflates two very different situations under one null value; a source_location (or similar evidence field) lets you tell "genuinely not in the document" apart from "present, but missed" — the second of which is an extraction bug worth fixing, unlike the first.
Not “Revert to required and rely on better prompting to make extraction …” — Requiring the field again brings back fabrication, and better prompting is probabilistic, so it cannot remove that incentive.
Not “Add a payment_method_confidence field so low-confidence nulls can…” — A confidence number on the field relies on self-reported confidence and still does not show whether the value was in the source.
Not “Default to the string "unknown" instead of null, so the field i…” — Defaulting to "unknown" hides both situations behind another placeholder, so missed values and truly absent ones stay indistinguishable.

questions.q: A single document has both receipt-like fields (vendor, total, date) and invoice-like fields (itemized line items, subtotal). Two purpose-built tools exist — extract_receipt and extract_invoice — and merging them would bloat both schemas. With tool_choice: "auto", the model sometimes picks receipt (losing line-item detail) and sometimes picks invoice (fabricating a PO number that doesn't exist on the document). The team needs both the line-item data and the receipt-style category field, without a bloated unified schema. What's the best design?
options: Merge into one universal schema, marking invoice-only fields as optional

Keep tool_choice: "any" with sharpened, non-overlapping descriptions distinguishing point-of-sale receipts from formal itemized invoices, and add a validation step: if the extraction doesn't match the detected document type, return a structured error and let the model retry against the corrected schema
Add a classify_document_type tool that must run first, before either extractor can be invoked
Keep tool_choice: "auto" and just add stronger prompt language about when each tool applies
questions.explain:
Sharpened, mutually exclusive tool descriptions reduce ambiguity up front, and a validation step that checks the extraction against the detected document type — returning a structured error and allowing a corrected retry when they don't match — handles the genuinely ambiguous cases that description quality alone won't fully resolve. A merged schema is explicitly what the team is trying to avoid.
Not “Merge into one universal schema, marking invoice-only fields as opt…” — One universal schema is what the team wants to avoid, since it bloats the structure and forces the model to guess which fields apply.
Not “Add a classify_document_type tool that must run first, before eit…” — A mandatory classification step adds a stage without solving how to detect a mismatched extraction, and the document is genuinely ambiguous.
Not “Keep tool_choice: "auto" and just add stronger prompt language ab…” — Stronger prompt language with "auto" stays probabilistic, so the model can still choose the wrong tool or skip tools altogether.

questions.q: A pipeline computes per-field confidence (amount 0.95, vendor 0.93, category 0.38, date 0.87) and an overall_confidence as their geometric mean (0.78), auto-approving anything above 0.75. An audit finds approved receipts where category confidence was as low as 0.32 (masked by high amount/vendor scores) and the category field was wrong in downstream processing — while receipts where every field sits around 0.72, yielding an overall_confidence of 0.72, are correctly categorized every time they're checked. What's the actual design flaw?
options: Geometric mean is the wrong statistic; switch to arithmetic mean instead

A single very low field can be masked by the rest and still cause a real downstream failure; use a minimum-field threshold (e.g., auto-approve only if every field individually clears 0.70) instead of any single aggregate statistic
Confidence scoring in general is unreliable here; replace it with a fixed percentage-based approval quota instead
The 0.75 threshold is simply too high; lowering it to 0.60 would reduce review workload without changing anything else
questions.explain:
A geometric mean lets one very weak field hide behind several strong ones, which is exactly how a category confidence of 0.32 got auto-approved. A minimum-field threshold ensures no single field is silently the weak link, which is why the flat-0.72-across-the-board receipts perform better in the audit despite a lower "overall" score.
Not “Geometric mean is the wrong statistic; switch to arithmetic mean in…” — Switching to an arithmetic mean still lets one very low field hide behind high ones, so the same masking flaw would continue.
Not “Confidence scoring in general is unreliable here; replace it with a…” — A fixed approval quota ignores actual field reliability, and abandoning confidence scoring discards a useful signal instead of fixing the aggregation.
Not “The 0.75 threshold is simply too high; lowering it to 0.60 would re…” — Lowering the threshold to 0.60 would approve even more receipts with weak fields, making the masked low-confidence problem worse.

questions.q: A vendor-name extraction repeatedly returns "AMZN" instead of "Amazon." A retry loop re-prompts with "always expand vendor names to their full legal name" and retries, but after five attempts on the same document, the model still returns an abbreviation roughly 20% of the time. On a different, unrelated validation failure ("vendor missing entirely"), a single retry with the error message resolves the issue 85% of the time. What does this contrast suggest, and what's the right fix for the abbreviation case specifically?
options: Increase retries to 10 for this category too — persistence eventually pays off

The model is reproducing a real-world abbreviation it has strong prior associations with, and re-prompting won't reliably override that; add a deterministic post-processing step — an alias lookup table (e.g., "AMZN" → "Amazon") — applied before downstream validation, instead of relying on the retry loop
This points to a model-capability gap; switch to a different model better suited to entity extraction
Treat any abbreviation as a hard validation failure and reject the extraction outright rather than retrying
questions.explain:
A retry loop that plateaus after several attempts, especially when contrasted against a different failure class where a single retry mostly works, indicates the model is drawing on a strong learned association ("AMZN") that re-prompting won't reliably override. A deterministic post-processing alias lookup handles it outside the retry loop, which is more reliable than continuing to ask nicely or discarding an otherwise-good extraction outright.
Not “Increase retries to 10 for this category too — persistence eventual…” — Ten retries would repeat an approach that has already plateaued after five attempts, so persistence is unlikely to remove the abbreviation.
Not “This points to a model-capability gap; switch to a different model …” — A single failure type that resolves easily on retry suggests the model is capable, so switching models is not warranted.
Not “Treat any abbreviation as a hard validation failure and reject the …” — Rejecting abbreviations outright discards otherwise good extractions, when a deterministic alias lookup can correct them.

questions.q: After 50,000 documents over three months, the pipeline's error tracking only records validation_failed: true/false — nothing about *why*. The team suspects failures cluster around specific vendors, date formats, or document types, but can't confirm it or prioritize fixes with the data they're currently logging. What should be added to enable systematic root-cause analysis?
options: A random UUID per extraction, to trace failures back to their source documents

A detected_pattern field describing what characteristic triggered the extraction path taken (e.g., "date_format_ddmmyyyy", "vendor_from_email_subject", "amount_with_currency_symbol"), so failures can be aggregated by pattern and the highest-impact ones prioritized
A retry_count field, to deprioritize documents that keep failing repeatedly
A model_version field, to compare accuracy across model updates over time
questions.explain:
A detected_pattern field capturing what characteristic drove a given extraction path is what turns a flat pass/fail log into something that can actually be aggregated and prioritized by root cause (vendor, date format, document type). A trace ID or retry count don't explain *why* a failure happened, only that one did.
Not “A random UUID per extraction, to trace failures back to their sourc…” — A random UUID lets you trace one record but does not describe why it failed, so failures cannot be grouped by cause.
Not “A retry_count field, to deprioritize documents that keep failing …” — A retry count shows how often something failed repeatedly, not what characteristic caused the failure, so it cannot reveal clusters.
Not “A model_version field, to compare accuracy across model updates o…” — A model version helps compare models over time but does not explain which vendors, date formats or document types are failing.

questions.q: Your support agent has an intake subagent that classifies incoming requests (simple: tracking/password/status | complex: refund/damage/billing), and an investigation subagent that handles complex cases. The intake subagent correctly marks requests as "simple" about 85% of the time, but 40% of requests marked simple still reach the investigation subagent, adding unnecessary latency. The system prompt says "skip investigation for simple cases," but logs show it's ignored. What's the most reliable fix?
options: Increase the intake classification model's temperature to make decisions more decisive
Add a step in the coordinator that reads the intake classification and only invokes the investigation subagent for cases marked complex
Include 5 few-shot examples in the intake prompt showing requests classified as simple
Increase the token budget for the intake subagent so it has more confidence in its decisions
questions.explain:
A system-prompt instruction ("skip investigation for simple cases") provides only probabilistic compliance. The reliable fix is a deterministic gate in the coordinator that simply never invokes the investigation subagent for cases the intake subagent already marked simple, enforcing the decision at the control-flow level instead of hoping the model follows a prose instruction.
Not “Increase the intake classification model's temperature to make deci…” — Temperature affects randomness in sampling, not whether a downstream step respects the classification. Investigation would still run for cases marked simple whenever the coordinator invokes it.
Not “Include 5 few-shot examples in the intake prompt showing requests c…” — Few-shot examples may sharpen classification, but the classification is already mostly right. The failure is that the result is ignored when deciding whether to invoke investigation.
Not “Increase the token budget for the intake subagent so it has more co…” — A bigger token budget gives the intake subagent room, not authority. The 40% leak happens after classification, where a control-flow check is missing.

questions.q: Your process_refund and request_refund_exception tools have descriptions: "Process a refund" and "Request an exception for refund eligibility." Both accept the same inputs (order_id, amount, reason). The agent calls the wrong one 25% of the time on policy-edge cases. You've already tried improving the descriptions with input formats, but misrouting persists. What's the next step on the fix ladder?
options: Add 8 few-shot examples showing correct tool selection for ambiguous cases
Rename request_refund_exception to escalate_refund_exception_review and add explicit "use this when policy does NOT allow the refund" guidance
Merge both tools into one and add an internal action: "approve" | "request_exception" input parameter
Split the tools into separate subagents, each with their own tool, to eliminate the choice entirely
questions.explain:
Once description improvements alone haven't resolved misrouting, renaming the ambiguous tool to make its purpose unmistakable — escalate_refund_exception_review, with explicit "use this when policy does NOT allow the refund" guidance — is the next rung on the fix ladder, ahead of merging tools with an internal parameter or splitting into separate subagents, both more disruptive changes.
Not “Add 8 few-shot examples showing correct tool selection for ambiguou…” — Examples are a later lever, and the tools take identical inputs and still sound alike. Fixing the naming and the "when policy does not allow" trigger is the cheaper next step.
Not “Merge both tools into one and add an internal `action: "approve" | …” — Merging both tools behind an internal action parameter is a more disruptive redesign that moves the same ambiguity into a parameter value instead of clarifying it.
Not “Split the tools into separate subagents, each with their own tool, …” — Splitting into separate subagents is a heavy architectural change. The next step is to make the exception tool's name and purpose unmistakable.

questions.q: After 12 turns investigating a disputed charge, your agent has verified the customer, retrieved three years of billing history, and identified the root issue ($200 overcharge on order #7743 from March). But when asked to "process the refund," it hesitates and asks "just to confirm, the order with the issue was...?" instead of recalling the specific order number. What's the problem, and how should it be fixed?
options: The model's context window is too small; increase it to preserve history better
Extract a persistent "case facts" block containing critical details (customer ID, order number, issue amount, dates) that's carried separately from the narrative conversation history
Reduce the number of turns allowed before summarization
Require the customer to re-state the order number before proceeding
questions.explain:
This is context loss in a long investigation: specific numbers and identifiers can fade from a narrative history even though the conversation is nominally still "about" the same case. A persistent case-facts block (customer ID, order number, amount, dates) carried separately from the narrative is the direct fix — more targeted than simply enlarging the context window or asking the customer to repeat themselves.
Not “The model's context window is too small; increase it to preserve hi…” — A larger window does not stop specific identifiers fading from a narrative history. The details need to be stored somewhere they cannot get lost.
Not “Reduce the number of turns allowed before summarization” — Summarising sooner would compress detail earlier and make the loss of the order number and amount more likely, not less.
Not “Require the customer to re-state the order number before proceeding” — Asking the customer to repeat the order number pushes the system's memory failure onto them and does not fix the underlying context loss.

questions.q: You've split the support system into a coordinator plus two subagents: one for order investigation and one for risk assessment. A case arrives: "I want a $500 refund due to damaged goods." Both subagents run, but the coordinator receives only risk-assessment findings ("Low risk, proceed") and no findings from the order-investigation subagent. Production logs show the order-investigation subagent ran but hit a backend timeout. The coordinator can't distinguish "no issues found" from "investigation failed," so it proceeds with incomplete information. What change would best solve this?
options: Restructure the case so order investigation always runs first, and risk assessment only if investigation succeeds
Require both subagents to output a status field indicating success/failure/partial, plus structured error context (errorCategory, isRetryable) when something goes wrong
Merge the two subagents into one
Add a retry loop in the coordinator that automatically re-invokes failed subagents
questions.explain:
When a subagent fails, the coordinator needs a structured signal to tell "nothing was found" apart from "the investigation itself failed." A status field (success/failure/partial) plus structured error context (errorCategory, isRetryable) gives the coordinator exactly that distinction; without it, a silent timeout can look identical to a clean negative result.
Not “Restructure the case so order investigation always runs first, and …” — Running investigation first still would not tell the coordinator whether it succeeded. A silent timeout would remain indistinguishable from a clean result.
Not “Merge the two subagents into one” — Merging the subagents does not fix the missing failure signal. A single agent could still hide a timeout behind a silent empty result.
Not “Add a retry loop in the coordinator that automatically re-invokes f…” — Automatic retries do not tell the coordinator what happened when retries fail, and they would not separate a clean negative from a failure.

questions.q: The MCP backend exposes tools that list available refund policies, approved return-reason codes, escalation-queue names, and supported regions. In production, every new case triggers 4 discovery tool calls to learn what exists, consuming roughly 800ms of latency before any customer-specific lookup happens. These lists change weekly but are read-only. Logs show the agent burns token budget on discovery before it can act. What's the most appropriate integration change?
options: Cache the tool outputs in a CLAUDE.md file so the agent reads them once
Expose these catalogs as MCP **resources** (URI-addressable reference data) rather than **tools**, so the agent can read them directly without consuming a model decision or a round-trip
Create a single get_system_metadata tool that returns all four catalogs at once
Require the agent to skip discovery entirely and rely on its training knowledge of policies
questions.explain:
Read-only, rarely-changing catalogs that exist to be discovered rather than acted upon belong in MCP resources, not tools — removing the round-trip decision cost entirely. Caching in CLAUDE.md still requires re-reading the catalogs into context every session, and merging into a single tool still costs a round-trip.
Not “Cache the tool outputs in a CLAUDE.md file so the agent reads the…” — A CLAUDE.md copy still must be loaded into context each session and goes stale as the lists change weekly, and it does not remove discovery calls.
Not “Create a single get_system_metadata tool that returns all four ca…” — One combined metadata tool still costs a round trip and a model decision per case, so the latency problem is only reduced, not removed.
Not “Require the agent to skip discovery entirely and rely on its traini…” — Policy and region catalogs that change weekly cannot be reliably recalled from training knowledge, so the agent would act on outdated or invented information.

questions.q: A case is escalated to a human agent with a 72% confidence score and a note saying "case seems complex." But investigation shows: customer identity is verified, order exists, refund window is open, damage evidence is clear, and refund amount is within policy. The escalation was triggered by an engineer's "confidence < 80% → escalate" rule. The confidence actually dropped to 72% only because the agent was uncertain whether a small warehouse fee was refundable, not because the case itself was complex. What's fundamentally wrong with this escalation signal?
options: The confidence threshold is too strict; raise it to 60%
Self-reported model confidence is poorly calibrated — it correlates weakly with actual case complexity and can be confidently wrong on the easiest cases while uncertain on genuinely simple ones
Confidence scores should be averaged across the whole case, not reported per-turn
Use turn count instead of confidence; escalate after 6 turns regardless of complexity
questions.explain:
Self-reported model confidence is a poorly calibrated proxy for actual case complexity — it can dip on a single unresolved sub-question even when every other part of the case is completely clear-cut, which is exactly what happened here. Escalation thresholds built on this signal will misfire in both directions: escalating clear cases and failing to escalate genuinely hard ones.
Not “The confidence threshold is too strict; raise it to 60%” — Moving the threshold to 60% does not make confidence reflect real complexity. The 72% was caused by one small unresolved question, so the signal itself is the problem.
Not “Confidence scores should be averaged across the whole case, not rep…” — Averaging confidence over the whole case still depends on a poorly calibrated self-reported number, so it does not fix the flawed signal.
Not “Use turn count instead of confidence; escalate after 6 turns regard…” — Turn count does not measure complexity either, since routine cases can need several turns while hard ones resolve quickly.

questions.q: A customer asks, "Can you process my refund now?" The agent's response includes a tool-use block for process_refund with correct parameters, but the response text also says "I've processed your refund — you should see it in 3–5 business days." The application's agentic loop terminates after seeing this final text and never executes the pending tool call, so the customer gets a confirmation message but no refund is actually issued. What's the design flaw?
options: The model should never generate customer-facing text in the same response as a tool call

The loop must check whether stop_reason is "tool_use" to know a tool call is pending; if so, it must execute the tool and continue the loop rather than treating the response as final just because text is also present
The response should be split into two separate API calls to avoid mixing concerns
Add a deterministic check for phrases like "processed" in the text to prevent premature loop termination
questions.explain:
The agentic loop must check whether stop_reason is "tool_use" to know a tool call is still pending, and execute it regardless of any accompanying text, rather than treating the presence of customer-facing text as a signal that nothing further needs to happen. Terminating early here means the tool call that should have processed the refund never actually runs.
Not “The model should never generate customer-facing text in the same re…” — Text alongside a tool call is normal. The flaw is how the loop interprets the response, not that the model produced customer-facing text.
Not “The response should be split into two separate API calls to avoid m…” — Splitting the response into two API calls adds complexity without changing that the loop must act on a pending tool call.
Not “Add a deterministic check for phrases like "processed" in the text …” — Scanning the text for phrases like "processed" is brittle and unrelated to whether a tool call is pending. stop_reason is the reliable signal.

questions.q: Production analysis shows an inverted pattern: simple requests (resend tracking link, password reset) are escalated 35% of the time, while complex policy cases (international damage claims, subscription billing disputes) are resolved autonomously 28% of the time — both wrong outcomes. Investigation reveals the agent escalates using a heuristic: "if the conversation has more than 5 turns, escalate." But simple cases often need 6–8 turns for data gathering (a customer didn't provide an order number initially, or an email needed clarifying), while some policy cases resolve in 3–4 turns given the right expertise. Why is this heuristic unreliable, and what should replace it?
options: Use conversation length but adjust the threshold per case type; simple cases get a higher turn limit

Escalation should be based on explicit, measurable criteria — policy ambiguity in the documentation, required customer data the customer can't provide, or conflicting information from backend systems — not proxy metrics like turn count
Escalate only when the model's confidence score drops below 50%
Always escalate cases with more than 4 tool calls, since tool-call count indicates complexity
questions.explain:
Turn count is a proxy that doesn't track actual complexity — a routine case can easily need extra turns just for data-gathering, while an expert can resolve a genuinely complex policy question in very few. Escalation should trigger on explicit, checkable conditions instead: policy ambiguity, missing customer-supplied data, or contradictory backend information.
Not “Use conversation length but adjust the threshold per case type; sim…” — Adjusting turn limits per case type keeps a proxy that does not measure complexity, so simple and complex cases would still be misrouted.
Not “Escalate only when the model's confidence score drops below 50%” — A 50% confidence cut-off relies on self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated and would also misroute simple and complex cases.
Not “Always escalate cases with more than 4 tool calls, since tool-call …” — Tool-call count is another proxy for complexity and would again escalate routine multi-step cases while missing genuinely complex ones.

questions.q: A coordinator invokes a refund-decision subagent with a highly prescriptive prompt: "Check if customer is verified AND order exists AND refund window is open AND damage evidence is provided. If all true, approve. If any false, escalate. If customer is verified but evidence is unclear, gather more details." On standard, well-documented cases this works, but on unusual cases (a customer claims damage but has no photo, or the return window is ambiguous due to international shipping), the subagent either escalates unnecessarily or asks for details the coordinator already tried to gather. What's the architectural flaw?
options: The subagent needs the full conversation history passed explicitly

The prompt over-specifies decision steps with rigid if-then-else logic, leaving no room for the subagent to reason about nuanced cases; it should instead receive investigation tools and clear decision criteria, but be allowed to assess independently whether those criteria are met
The coordinator should call a different subagent for unusual cases
The refund-decision subagent shouldn't have access to investigation tools at all
questions.explain:
A rigid, fully-enumerated if-then-else prompt leaves the subagent no room to reason when a real case doesn't map cleanly onto the enumerated conditions (missing photo evidence, ambiguous international shipping windows). The better design gives the subagent the same investigation tools and the underlying decision criteria, but lets it assess whether those criteria are satisfied given what it can actually observe, rather than forcing an exact literal match.
Not “The subagent needs the full conversation history passed explicitly” — Passing the full history would not fix the core issue, which is that the prompt enumerates rigid conditions that unusual cases cannot match.
Not “The coordinator should call a different subagent for unusual cases” — Routing unusual cases to a different subagent does not remove the brittle if-then logic and requires predicting every unusual case in advance.
Not “The refund-decision subagent shouldn't have access to investigation…” — Removing investigation tools would leave the subagent unable to assess cases itself, which makes the over-escalation worse.

questions.q: A /refactor-tests skill encodes a company's standard test-refactoring pattern. It was originally created at ~/.claude/skills/refactor-tests/SKILL.md to test locally. Now 40 engineers need to use it consistently. What's wrong with the current location, and what's the correct migration path?
options: Personal skills are faster; keep it at the user level and have each engineer copy the file manually to their own machine

The user-level location is personal and not version-controlled; the skill should move to .claude/skills/refactor-tests/SKILL.md in the repo so every engineer inherits it via git and uses identical logic
Create a duplicate at the project level while keeping the user-level version, so team members can use either
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since skills can't be shared across a team
questions.explain:
User-level configuration is personal and never shared through version control, no matter how good the skill is. Making a skill available consistently to 40 engineers means it has to live at the project level, where every clone of the repo inherits the identical file — not duplicated in two places or manually distributed.
Not “Personal skills are faster; keep it at the user level and have each…” — The user-level copy stays personal. Having every engineer copy it by hand is error-prone and lets versions drift, which defeats consistent use.
Not “Create a duplicate at the project level while keeping the user-leve…” — Keeping two copies invites the two versions to diverge, so engineers may end up running different logic.
Not “Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since skills can't …” — Skills can be shared across a team when placed at the project level, so converting to a slash command is unnecessary.

questions.q: A skill spawns a subagent with context: fork to explore third-party API documentation and produce a long reference document summarizing it. When control returns to the main session, the developer asks Claude to use that reference for code generation, and Claude says it has no knowledge of any such reference. What's the underlying issue?
options: context: fork writes to an isolated temporary sandbox, and any file the fork creates never exists outside it

A forked subagent's internal reasoning and any artifacts it produced are not automatically available to the parent session; whatever the fork returns as its final result must be explicitly passed back as context (or written somewhere the main session actually reads) for the main session to use it
Subagents are not permitted to produce long-form output when context: fork is set
The reference exists, but the developer must use a memory-inspection command to view fork-isolated outputs
questions.explain:
A forked subagent's internal reasoning and any artifacts it generates don't automatically flow back to the parent session — only whatever the fork explicitly returns as its result does. If the main session needs the reference material, it has to be passed back directly or written somewhere the main session actually reads, not just produced somewhere inside the fork.
Not “context: fork writes to an isolated temporary sandbox, and any fi…” — A fork is not a sandbox that destroys its output. What the fork returns can be passed back explicitly, so the gap is about transferring results, not about files vanishing.
Not “Subagents are not permitted to produce long-form output when `conte…” — Nothing limits forked subagents to short output. It could produce a long reference, but the main session still has to be handed that result.
Not “The reference exists, but the developer must use a memory-inspectio…” — No special inspection command exposes fork-isolated work to the parent. The result has to be passed back or saved where the main session reads.

questions.q: A developer is implementing a distributed caching layer in a service they've never worked with before. They ask Claude to implement it directly, with a long, detailed prompt describing the desired behavior. After review, they discover the design doesn't account for TTL-based expiry, an important pattern in that service, forcing a rework. On a second, similar task in the same unfamiliar service, they instead ask Claude to first surface open design questions before writing any code; Claude asks about TTL handling, consistency guarantees, and cache scope, all of which shape the eventual implementation. Why did this approach work better here?
options: Interviewing Claude before implementation always produces objectively better code, regardless of context

In an unfamiliar domain where the relevant tradeoffs and constraints aren't already known, surfacing design questions before coding catches gaps that a single detailed upfront prompt is likely to miss, since the prompt-writer doesn't yet know what they don't know
The interview approach is faster because it skips implementation
The interview approach forces more thorough documentation as a side effect
questions.explain:
The interview pattern earns its value specifically in unfamiliar territory, where the person writing the prompt doesn't yet know which tradeoffs matter (like TTL-based expiry here) and so can't have specified them upfront. Surfacing design questions before implementation catches exactly the kind of gap that a single detailed prompt — however thorough it feels — is likely to miss when the domain itself is the unknown.
Not “Interviewing Claude before implementation always produces objective…” — Interviewing is not always better. Its value depends on the domain being unfamiliar, so a blanket claim of better code ignores that.
Not “The interview approach is faster because it skips implementation” — Surfacing questions does not skip implementation. It happens before coding, and its payoff is catching missing design considerations, not speed.
Not “The interview approach forces more thorough documentation as a side…” — Better documentation may result, but it is not why the approach worked. The benefit was exposing the TTL and consistency considerations.

questions.q: A developer is refactoring a function signature used across 30 files and updating its 15 call sites. After 12 files, they discover the new signature breaks an edge case they hadn't planned for and need to work out a fix. Should they fork the session to explore the fix, or keep working in the main session?
options: Fork the session to explore the fix in isolation, then bring the result back into the main refactoring

Continue in the main session — it retains full context of the 12 files already changed, avoiding lost work; forking here would isolate the fix but strip away the surrounding refactoring context the fix actually needs
Restart the whole task from scratch with updated requirements
Forking is only appropriate for documentation work, never for code changes
questions.explain:
Continuing in the main session preserves the accumulated context of the 12 files already changed, which the fix genuinely depends on; forking at this point would isolate the fix into a context that's missing exactly the surrounding refactoring work it needs to stay consistent with.
Not “Fork the session to explore the fix in isolation, then bring the re…” — Forking would isolate the fix from the accumulated work on the 12 changed files, which the fix needs to remain consistent with.
Not “Restart the whole task from scratch with updated requirements” — Restarting from scratch discards the 12 files already changed and wastes that work when the main session can carry on.
Not “Forking is only appropriate for documentation work, never for code …” — Forking is not limited to documentation. It is a general tool, but here its isolation would cost context the fix depends on.

questions.q: A .claude/rules/api-validation.md file has frontmatter paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"], containing rules about validating all API inputs. A developer creates src/api-client/index.ts — a sibling directory, not a subdirectory of src/api/ — and asks Claude to implement an API client there. The validation rules never apply to this file. Why?
options: The glob src/api/**/*.ts only matches paths under src/api/; src/api-client/ is a different directory that happens to share a name prefix, so the pattern simply doesn't match it — a broader pattern would be needed to cover both
.claude/rules/ files only apply to files that already existed when the session started
Glob patterns are case-sensitive and the path casing doesn't match
Rule paths require an exact directory match, and sibling directories are always excluded by design
questions.explain:
Glob matching is literal path matching: src/api/**/*.ts matches only paths that actually fall under src/api/, and src/api-client/ is a distinct sibling directory that happens to share a prefix, not a match for that pattern. A broader pattern (or an additional rule) would be needed to cover both directories.
Not “.claude/rules/ files only apply to files that already existed whe…” — Path-scoped rules are not limited to files that existed when the session started. The pattern simply does not match this sibling directory.
Not “Glob patterns are case-sensitive and the path casing doesn't match” — Case sensitivity is not the problem. The directory name api-client is a different path from api and not a casing mismatch.
Not “Rule paths require an exact directory match, and sibling directorie…” — Rule paths do not require an exact directory match or exclude siblings by design. A pattern matches whatever paths its glob covers, so a broader glob can include both.

questions.q: A developer spends four hours refactoring a component library. Two hours in, Claude reads and correctly restates an explicit architectural constraint: "all async operations must use Suspense; no raw promises directly in JSX." At hour four, asked to add a new async feature, Claude writes a component that awaits a promise directly inside a useEffect, violating that constraint without comment. The developer points it out, Claude fixes it, and then the same category of violation resurfaces an hour later in a different component. What would most reliably prevent this recurrence?
options: Restart the session every two hours to keep context "fresh"

Maintain a scratchpad file (e.g., a running constraints doc) recording critical architectural invariants as they're discovered, and have Claude reference it before generating new async code — giving the constraint a durable source of truth instead of relying on it staying salient in a long, growing conversation
Run a context-compaction command every hour regardless of what's happening
Ask Claude to restate the constraint out loud every 30 minutes
questions.explain:
A running scratchpad of architectural constraints, checked before generating new code in the affected area, gives a long session a durable place for a constraint to live outside the conversation's own "salience," which is what silently erodes as the session grows and moves on to new topics. Restarting periodically or compacting on a fixed schedule don't specifically preserve this kind of constraint — they just change what else gets lost along with it.
Not “Restart the session every two hours to keep context "fresh"” — Restarting every two hours loses the context built up and does not preserve the architectural constraint across the new session.
Not “Run a context-compaction command every hour regardless of what's ha…” — Compaction on a schedule can discard the constraint along with other detail, so it does not reliably keep it available.
Not “Ask Claude to restate the constraint out loud every 30 minutes” — Asking Claude to restate the rule periodically relies on the model recalling it, and a restatement does not give a durable source to check before writing code.

questions.q: A coordinator needs to explore two mutually exclusive research hypotheses at once: one line of investigation assuming "policy X accelerates adoption" and another assuming "policy X has no measurable effect." Using ordinary named subagents, each spawned fresh with only its own hypothesis in its prompt, the coordinator still finds that reasoning clearly built on one hypothesis leaks into the write-up for the other — findings that should only make sense under "accelerates" show up justifying "no effect" too. What's the most direct fix for exploring genuinely incompatible branches like this?
options: Add allowedTools: ["Task"] to the coordinator's configuration, since parallel spawn requires it

Fork the session at the point where the branches diverge, so each hypothesis is explored in its own isolated copy of the accumulated investigation state, then compare the two forks' conclusions afterward
Parallel Task calls cannot accept differing prompts; switch to strictly sequential delegation instead
Have the synthesis agent automatically detect and remove cross-hypothesis contamination after the fact
questions.explain:
Forking at the point where two genuinely incompatible investigations diverge gives each hypothesis its own isolated copy of the shared context to build on independently, preventing conclusions grounded in one hypothesis from leaking into the other's write-up. Ordinary fresh named subagents don't solve this on their own if the coordinator's framing or the shared setup still lets assumptions bleed across branches.
Not “Add allowedTools: ["Task"] to the coordinator's configuration, si…” — Adding Task to allowedTools only enables spawning subagents. It does nothing to stop one hypothesis's reasoning leaking into the other's write-up.
Not “Parallel Task calls cannot accept differing prompts; switch to st…” — Parallel Task calls can take different prompts, and sequential delegation would not isolate the branches from each other.
Not “Have the synthesis agent automatically detect and remove cross-hypo…” — Cleaning up contamination after the fact is unreliable. The branches should be separated from the moment they diverge.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates "research the EU's approach to a regulatory topic" to a named search subagent, and later delegates "research the US's approach to the same regulatory topic" to that same subagent. In between, the coordinator's own conversation has built up 15 turns of discussion establishing shared terminology and which document sources are authoritative for this topic. The second delegation comes back sparse and generic, as if the subagent doesn't share any of that established framing. What's the most accurate explanation?
options: Subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's full conversation history, so the sparseness must mean the second request itself was too narrow

A subagent only receives what's explicitly included in its own invocation prompt; context the coordinator built up in its own conversation — terminology, source guidance — isn't automatically available to a subagent unless the coordinator restates it in that subagent's prompt
The first delegation exhausted the subagent's usable sources, degrading the second
Subagents share a temporary memory keyed by topic, but that memory had already expired between the two delegations
questions.explain:
A subagent only has what's explicitly included in its own invocation prompt. Terminology and source guidance the coordinator built up in its own conversation over 15 turns doesn't automatically travel with a new delegation — it has to be restated in that subagent's prompt, which is exactly what was missing here.
Not “Subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's full conversation…” — Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history. The sparse result points to missing context in the prompt, not a narrow request.
Not “The first delegation exhausted the subagent's usable sources, degra…” — Nothing suggests sources were exhausted. The result lacked the terminology and source guidance that was never passed in.
Not “Subagents share a temporary memory keyed by topic, but that memory …” — Subagents do not share a topic-keyed memory that expires, so there is no such store to blame for the generic answer.

questions.q: A synthesis agent constantly needs to fact-check small claims mid-report — "is 2023 the right year for that report," "did that agency actually issue this," "is this within the stated margin of error." Every check currently routes through the coordinator to a full-capability search subagent, adding a few seconds of round-trip latency each time, and the synthesis agent makes 80+ such checks per report. What tool-distribution change is most appropriate?
options: Give the synthesis agent unrestricted access to the same web-search and document-analysis tools the other subagents use

Give the synthesis agent one narrow, scoped tool built specifically for quick single-fact verification, so the common case resolves locally, while genuinely complex verification still routes through the coordinator
Batch all 80+ checks into one large request sent to the coordinator at the very end
Remove fact verification from the synthesis step entirely to save latency
questions.explain:
A narrow, purpose-built verification tool for simple single-fact checks lets the high-frequency, low-complexity case resolve locally without a coordinator round-trip, while genuinely complex verification still goes through the coordinator. Giving the synthesis agent full search/analysis tool access reintroduces the coordination and scope problems that scoped tools are meant to avoid.
Not “Give the synthesis agent unrestricted access to the same web-search…” — Unrestricted search access gives the synthesis agent tools outside its specialisation, which invites misuse and scope problems.
Not “Batch all 80+ checks into one large request sent to the coordinator…” — Batching 80+ checks to the end delays catching errors and does not remove the per-check round-trip cost during synthesis.
Not “Remove fact verification from the synthesis step entirely to save l…” — Removing fact checks to save time lets small factual errors through, trading accuracy for speed instead of making checks cheaper.

questions.q: A research pipeline runs parallel subagents, then sends their combined output straight to a report-writing step with no intermediate check. Reviewers later find citation mismatches (a claim attributed to one source that actually came from another) and outright contradictions between two sections of the same report. Every individual subagent's own output looks reasonable in isolation. Where is the defect, and what's the most effective fix?
options: One specific subagent must have misattributed a source; re-run that subagent with stricter instructions
The report-writing step is introducing the citation errors itself; add a citation-cleanup pass after report generation
Add an explicit coordinator-level checkpoint that evaluates the combined findings against citation-accuracy and cross-section-consistency criteria before handing off to report generation
The problem is in how tool responses format citations; normalize citation format with a hook
questions.explain:
Every subagent looking correct in isolation doesn't guarantee the combined output is coherent — that's exactly why an explicit checkpoint evaluating the aggregated findings against citation-accuracy and cross-section-consistency criteria, before report generation runs, catches problems that no individual subagent would ever surface on its own.
Not “One specific subagent must have misattributed a source; re-run that…” — Every subagent's output looks fine on its own, so nothing indicates one subagent misattributed a source. The problem appears only when results are combined.
Not “The report-writing step is introducing the citation errors itself; …” — The cleanup after report generation catches errors too late, and the mismatches arise from combining findings that were never checked together beforehand.
Not “The problem is in how tool responses format citations; normalize ci…” — Citation format normalisation addresses presentation, not whether claims are attributed to the right source or whether sections contradict each other.

questions.q: A coordinator launches three subagents in parallel — search, document analysis, and synthesis — for a request that fundamentally depends on reconciling conflicting findings across topics. Search and document analysis both succeed; synthesis crashes partway through with an unrecoverable internal error.
