The coordinator now has two successful results and one hard failure, for a task where the missing synthesis step was the part actually responsible for resolving the conflicts the user asked about. What should the coordinator do?
options: Always return the two successful results as a partial report, since some information is better than none

Reason about whether the failed piece was essential to what was actually asked — since here the synthesis step was the entire point (reconciling conflicts), a partial report without it would misrepresent the state of the research, so this case should escalate rather than quietly return partial output
Retry the synthesis step exactly once more and return whatever it produces, succeed or fail
Discard everything and start the whole three-subagent pipeline over
questions.explain:
The right call depends on whether the failed piece was essential to what was actually asked. Here, reconciling conflicts across topics was the entire point of the request, and synthesis was the step responsible for that — so a "successful" partial report from just search and document analysis would misrepresent whether the actual question got answered, and escalating is more honest than quietly returning an incomplete result.
Not “Always return the two successful results as a partial report, since…” — Returning a partial report without the reconciliation the user asked for would suggest the question was answered when it was not.
Not “Retry the synthesis step exactly once more and return whatever it p…” — One retry returning whatever happens does not account for whether the missing piece was essential, so a failed retry could still yield a misleading output.
Not “Discard everything and start the whole three-subagent pipeline over” — Discarding the successful search and analysis results wastes valid work, and restarting does not address whether the failure is recoverable.

questions.q: A document-analysis subagent is scoped to extract findings only from a fixed, pre-approved set of internal PDFs. To let it double-check facts against the source text, it's given general-purpose web-search access as well. Within weeks, logs show it routinely uses that web-search access to pull in and cite outside sources the coordinator never approved, expanding scope well past the original document set. What's the most direct fix?
options: Remove web search entirely and tell the subagent, via the system prompt, to rely only on the approved documents
Replace the general web-search tool with a narrowly scoped verification tool that can only check claims against the specific approved document set, not the open web
Add a stronger prompt warning against using search to expand scope
Let the coordinator strip out any external citations from the subagent's output after the fact
questions.explain:
The scope-creep problem is a tool-design problem, not a prompting problem: replacing general web search with a tool that can only verify claims against the already-approved document set makes scope expansion structurally impossible, rather than relying on the model to voluntarily stay within bounds it technically still has the power to exceed.
Not “Remove web search entirely and tell the subagent, via the system pr…” — Removing web search and relying on a prompt instruction still depends on the model complying, and it loses the ability to verify against the approved sources.
Not “Add a stronger prompt warning against using search to expand scope” — A stronger prompt warning is advisory only, so the subagent can still use general search to pull in outside sources.
Not “Let the coordinator strip out any external citations from the subag…” — Stripping citations afterward treats the symptom, since the subagent still uses unapproved material in its reasoning.

questions.q: A multi-day research session is interrupted right after the search subagent finishes but before document analysis begins. The team wants to resume without re-running search from scratch. They restart the coordinator, and it sends document analysis a fresh prompt describing the new task — but never tells it what search already found. What's the most maintainable way to resume this kind of interrupted pipeline?
options: Just resume and let document analysis redo any lookups it needs; some redundant work is an acceptable tradeoff

Have each subagent export its completed state to a known location as it finishes, and have the coordinator load a manifest of that state on resume, re-injecting whatever a subsequent step actually needs
Manually copy-paste the search subagent's raw output into every future prompt for the rest of the session
Discard everything from before the interruption and start the whole pipeline over
questions.explain:
Structured state exports plus a coordinator-loaded manifest on resume is the reliable crash/interruption-recovery pattern: each subagent's completed work is captured in a known location, and resuming means loading that manifest and re-injecting only what a subsequent step actually needs, rather than redoing work or manually threading raw output through every future prompt.
Not “Just resume and let document analysis redo any lookups it needs; so…” — Redoing lookups wastes time and may produce different results than the earlier search, which the user wanted to avoid repeating.
Not “Manually copy-paste the search subagent's raw output into every fut…” — Pasting raw output into every future prompt is manual, bloats context, and is easy to forget or get wrong.
Not “Discard everything from before the interruption and start the whole…” — Starting over throws away the completed search work, defeating the goal of resuming without rerunning it.

questions.q: A team completes a multi-day research project on a fast-moving regulatory topic, citing a dozen sources. Two weeks later, they resume the same line of research to expand on one sub-topic, and simply re-inject all the prior findings as-is into the new session before continuing. A week after publishing the expanded report, they learn that two of the originally-cited sources have since been formally retracted or substantially revised, and the report's now-outdated claims are actively misleading readers. What practice would have caught this before publication?
options: Store every source as a permanent, stable URL so readers can always find the original text themselves

When resuming research after a significant time gap, explicitly validate whether previously-cited sources are still current before re-using them, rather than re-injecting old findings wholesale and treating them as still authoritative
Have a policy of never citing anything more than six months old
Re-run the entire original research pipeline from scratch every time any new work touches the same topic
questions.explain:
Time-sensitive research doesn't stay valid forever; resuming after a real time gap and re-injecting old findings as if they're still current risks exactly this outcome — publishing on sources that have since been retracted or substantially revised. Explicitly validating source currency before reuse, rather than treating a prior session's findings as permanently authoritative, is what would have caught it.
Not “Store every source as a permanent, stable URL so readers can always…” — Stable URLs let readers find the original text but do not tell the team whether a cited source has since been retracted or revised.
Not “Have a policy of never citing anything more than six months old” — A fixed age cutoff is arbitrary. A recent source can be retracted, and an older one can still be valid.
Not “Re-run the entire original research pipeline from scratch every tim…” — Rerunning the whole pipeline each time is wasteful and does not specifically check whether earlier sources are still current.

questions.q: An agent explores a repository using an MCP tool for definition lookup and another for call-site discovery. Some calls fail during a long exploration session, and the integration currently returns every failure as {"isError": true, "message": "Tool unavailable"}, whether the cause is a transient network blip, a malformed query, or a rate limit. The agent retries every failure the same way, sometimes looping for a long time on a query that will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried. What must be added to the tool responses to fix the retry logic?
options: Raise the maximum retry count and add exponential backoff uniformly across all retried calls
Log additional detail in the failure message so a human can read it later
Add an errorCategory (e.g. transient / validation / permission) and an isRetryable boolean to each error response, so the agent can distinguish a worthwhile retry from a hopeless one
Remove the retry mechanism entirely and fail immediately on any error
questions.explain:
An errorCategory plus an isRetryable flag lets the agent tell a worthwhile retry (transient) apart from a hopeless one (a malformed query that will fail identically every time). Without that distinction, uniform retry logic burns time on exactly the calls retrying can never fix, and failing immediately on everything throws away the retries that would have actually succeeded.
Not “Raise the maximum retry count and add exponential backoff uniformly…” — More retries with uniform backoff would keep retrying calls that can never succeed, such as a malformed query, wasting time.
Not “Log additional detail in the failure message so a human can read it…” — A more readable message for a human does not give the agent a structured signal it can act on in its retry logic.
Not “Remove the retry mechanism entirely and fail immediately on any error” — Failing immediately on every error discards transient failures that would succeed on retry, so recoverable calls would be lost.

questions.q: A shared catalog of approved integrations (REST APIs, webhook destinations, supported SDK versions) is exposed as an MCP tool, list_integrations. During a typical 2-hour exploration session, the agent calls this tool 15+ times just to check what's available, and each call consumes a tool-use decision step even though the underlying list rarely changes within a session. What's the most efficient way to expose this catalog?
options: Merge several related discovery tools into one larger tool with a more detailed description
Cache the tool's output into CLAUDE.md so the agent can reference it as static project memory
Expose the integration catalog as an MCP **resource** rather than a tool, so it can be read directly without spending a tool-use decision each time
Add the integration list as literal text in the system prompt
questions.explain:
A catalog that's mostly static within a session and exists to be looked up, not acted on, is a textbook fit for an MCP resource — it can be read directly without spending a tool-use decision on every check. Caching into CLAUDE.md still requires a file read each time it's needed and goes stale silently; a single combined tool still costs a round trip per call.
Not “Merge several related discovery tools into one larger tool with a m…” — Merging discovery tools still costs a round trip per call, so the agent keeps spending decision steps on a static list.
Not “Cache the tool's output into CLAUDE.md so the agent can reference…” — A CLAUDE.md copy would need to be maintained by hand and goes stale silently when the catalogue changes, and it is not the natural mechanism for reference data.
Not “Add the integration list as literal text in the system prompt” — Hard-coding the list into the system prompt makes it static text that must be edited whenever it changes and bloats every request.

questions.q: During analysis, an agent needs the contents of three unrelated source files as baseline context before proposing any changes. It currently reads file A, waits for the result, reads file B, waits, then reads file C — three sequential tool-use round trips for three independent, non-dependent reads. What change improves efficiency here without changing what's actually being read?
options: Use a single Bash command to concatenate all three files with a shell glob instead of using the file-reading tool
Emit all three read calls together in one response, as separate tool-use blocks, so the client can execute them concurrently and return all three results at once
Split the analysis across three separate sessions, one file per session
Keep reading sequentially, but cache each file's contents locally to avoid reading it again later
questions.explain:
When several reads are genuinely independent of each other, emitting them together as separate tool-use blocks in one response lets the client run them concurrently and return all results at once, rather than paying three sequential round trips for work that never depended on being sequential in the first place.
Not “Use a single Bash command to concatenate all three files with a she…” — Using a shell command to concatenate files gives up the dedicated read tool and does not make the reads concurrent in the intended way.
Not “Split the analysis across three separate sessions, one file per ses…” — Spreading one analysis across three sessions fragments context, when the files are needed together as baseline context.
Not “Keep reading sequentially, but cache each file's contents locally t…” — Caching file contents does not remove the three sequential round trips for the first read of each independent file.

questions.q: One MCP database tool returns {"isError": true, "errorCategory": "transient", "isRetryable": true} on one call and {"isError": true, "errorCategory": "validation", "isRetryable": false} on a different call. If the agent's recovery logic treats every error identically and simply retries both the same way, what actually happens?
options: Both eventually succeed on retry; the transient one just takes a bit longer

The transient failure may well succeed on retry, but the validation failure (a malformed query, say) will keep failing identically every time, since retrying with the same bad input doesn't fix the input — wasting attempts and context on a call retrying can't help
Both fail regardless, and the agent should escalate both to a human immediately
Neither will ever succeed, so all retries should simply be disabled everywhere
questions.explain:
Treating every error identically wastes effort specifically on the validation failure, since retrying the same malformed input produces the same malformed result every time — only the transient failure has any real chance of resolving on retry. The fix isn't fewer or more retries across the board, it's recognizing which category is actually retryable.
Not “Both eventually succeed on retry; the transient one just takes a bi…” — If every failure is retried the same way, both would eventually be treated as recoverable, but the validation failure never succeeds because the input stays bad.
Not “Both fail regardless, and the agent should escalate both to a human…” — The transient failure may well succeed on retry, so both do not fail regardless. Treating both the same wastes effort on only one.
Not “Neither will ever succeed, so all retries should simply be disabled…” — Disabling retries everywhere throws away the transient case, which can succeed, so the answer is to distinguish categories.

questions.q: A developer-productivity agent has 22 tools available at once: 5 built-ins, 12 MCP tools for various kinds of code search (keyword search, cross-reference lookup, type-hierarchy exploration, and more), and 5 more for generating boilerplate. Logs show the agent occasionally reaches for a slower, more generic search tool when a faster, more specific one would clearly have been better — even after descriptions were already improved. What's the next lever to pull?
options: Cut the least-used tools until the total count is 10 or fewer
Switch to a model with a larger context window so tool-selection reasoning has more room

Narrow which tools are actually available per task type — e.g. an exploration-focused pass gets only a handful of high-signal search tools, while an implementation-focused pass gets the editing and boilerplate tools — reducing the live decision space itself rather than relying on ever-better descriptions alone
Build a separate preprocessing step that decides which tool to call before the agent ever sees the request
questions.explain:
Narrowing which tools are actually available for a given task phase reduces the live decision space itself, which is a more direct fix for misselection among 22 similar-looking tools than hoping ever-better descriptions alone will fully resolve it, or assuming a bigger context window somehow improves the underlying selection judgment.
Not “Cut the least-used tools until the total count is 10 or fewer” — Cutting to ten tools is arbitrary and removes capabilities the agent still needs, instead of narrowing the set for each task phase.
Not “Switch to a model with a larger context window so tool-selection re…” — A larger context window does not improve the agent's judgment in choosing between similar tools, so misselection would continue.
Not “Build a separate preprocessing step that decides which tool to call…” — A separate preprocessing step to pick tools adds a brittle routing layer, when scoping the tools available per phase is simpler.

questions.q: A system requires that all file modifications stay within an explicitly approved workspace_root directory. A developer asks an agent to "clean up unused dependencies," and without any programmatic boundary check in place, the agent occasionally ends up running Bash commands that touch directories outside that approved root. What is the most reliable way to enforce this boundary?
options: Add a hook that runs after the Bash command completes, checking whether it touched an out-of-scope path and rolling back if so
Have the agent itself run a path-check command before the real modification, as a self-imposed safeguard
Add a prompt instruction stating the boundary rule and monitor logs afterward for any violations
Add a hook that runs *before* the Bash tool executes, validates the target path against workspace_root, and blocks the command outright with feedback if it falls outside that boundary
questions.explain:
A hook that runs before the Bash tool executes and can validate the target path against workspace_root — blocking the call outright when it falls outside — is the only one of these options that can actually prevent an out-of-scope modification from happening. A post-hoc check or a self-imposed pre-check the agent might skip both allow the violation to occur first; a prompt instruction is advisory, not enforced.
Not “Add a hook that runs after the Bash command completes, checking whe…” — A check after the command finishes lets the out-of-scope modification happen first, and rolling back may not undo every side effect.
Not “Have the agent itself run a path-check command before the real modi…” — A self-imposed path check depends on the agent choosing to run it, so it can be skipped, which is the failure in the first place.
Not “Add a prompt instruction stating the boundary rule and monitor logs…” — A prompt rule with after-the-fact log monitoring is advisory, so violations still occur before anyone notices them.

questions.q: An MCP tool call returns an error with errorCategory: "permission". What does this most likely indicate, and what should the agent do next?
options: The operation timed out and will likely succeed if retried with backoff

The agent lacks sufficient authorization for this operation (missing credentials or an insufficient scope); retrying the same call won't change that outcome, so the right move is to escalate, request different credentials, or skip the operation rather than keep retrying
The input was malformed and should be reformatted before retrying
The operation actually succeeded, just with an empty result, and can be treated as a no-op
questions.explain:
A "permission" error category signals an authorization problem — missing credentials or an insufficient scope — which retrying the identical call will never resolve. The right response is to escalate, obtain different credentials, or skip the operation, not to keep retrying as if the failure might eventually clear on its own.
Not “The operation timed out and will likely succeed if retried with bac…” — A timeout is a transient failure that suits retry with backoff, whereas a permission error indicates the agent is not authorised.
Not “The input was malformed and should be reformatted before retrying” — A malformed input is a validation error. A permission error means authorisation is missing, so reformatting the input will not help.
Not “The operation actually succeeded, just with an empty result, and ca…” — A permission error is a failure, not a successful empty result, so treating it as a no-op would hide that the operation was blocked.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates codebase analysis across three subagents — one traces API handlers, one traces database writes, one analyzes tests — and each returns its findings as free-form prose summaries. When an implementation-focused step later tries to act on those summaries, it struggles to cite exact file paths, line numbers, or code snippets, since the prose only describes what was found in general terms. What change most improves reliability downstream?
options: Have the coordinator manually go back through the prose afterward and try to reconstruct file paths and line numbers from it
Reduce the number of subagents to one or two so there's less to reconcile

Require each subagent to return structured findings — the claim, the exact file path, a line range, and a short source excerpt — instead of unstructured prose, so precise attribution survives all the way through to the implementation step
Merge every subagent's findings into a single combined document and have the implementation step search for the referenced code itself
questions.explain:
Structured findings (claim, file path, line range, source excerpt) preserve exactly the precision that free-form prose summaries lose — without them, a later step has to try to reconstruct file-level detail from a paragraph that was never designed to carry it. Manually reconstructing that detail after the fact is error-prone and doesn't scale, and merging everything into one document doesn't restore detail that was never captured in the first place.
Not “Have the coordinator manually go back through the prose afterward a…” — Reconstructing file paths and line numbers from prose afterward is error-prone, and details that were never captured cannot be recovered reliably.
Not “Reduce the number of subagents to one or two so there's less to rec…” — Fewer subagents does not stop each from returning vague prose, so the downstream step would still lack exact locations.
Not “Merge every subagent's findings into a single combined document and…” — Combining everything into a single document and making the implementation step search again discards detail that the subagents already found.

questions.q: A team wants a slash command that only ever operates on files matching a specific pattern (e.g., generated API client files under a particular directory), regardless of which developer runs it or what else is open in their session. They configure this by adding disallowedTools to the command's own definition to block file types outside that pattern. In testing, the command still successfully edits files outside the intended pattern when a developer runs it from a broader working context. What's actually going wrong?
options: disallowedTools blocks entire tools (like Edit or Write) from being used at all — it has no concept of restricting a tool to only certain file paths, so it cannot enforce a pattern-based boundary on its own; a path-based restriction needs to be enforced elsewhere, such as through a hook that inspects the target path before allowing the edit
disallowedTools only applies to MCP tools, never to built-in tools like Edit and Write
The command definition is being overridden by a broader project-level configuration every time
disallowedTools requires an accompanying allowed-tools entry to take effect at all
questions.explain:
disallowedTools operates at the level of whole tools, not individual file paths within a tool's use — it can prevent Edit from being used at all, but it has no mechanism for saying "only allow edits to files matching this pattern." Enforcing a path-based restriction requires something that actually inspects the target path before the edit happens, such as a hook, not a tool-level allow/deny list.
Not “disallowedTools only applies to MCP tools, never to built-in tool…” — disallowedTools is not limited to MCP tools and can block built-in tools. The problem is that it works at the level of whole tools.
Not “The command definition is being overridden by a broader project-lev…” — Nothing suggests a broader configuration is overriding the command. The behaviour follows from disallowedTools having no concept of file path patterns.
Not “disallowedTools requires an accompanying allowed-tools entry to…” — disallowedTools does not need an accompanying allowed-tools entry. Even then it still could not restrict edits by path pattern.

questions.q: A developer-productivity agent needs to hand off from a broad, exploratory investigation phase to a narrow, high-precision code-modification phase for the same task, without losing the context gathered during exploration. Using two entirely separate agent definitions with no shared context would solve the tool-scoping problem but would also force the modification phase to start blind. What approach best preserves context while still narrowing tool access for the second phase?
options: Keep a single agent and rely on prompt instructions to describe which tools are appropriate for which phase, without changing what's actually available

Delegate the modification phase to a subagent that receives the exploration phase's key findings explicitly in its invocation prompt, and is scoped to a narrower toolset appropriate for making the actual edits — preserving continuity through the handoff while still tightening tool access for the higher-risk phase
Run the whole task in one phase with all tools available throughout, since narrowing access isn't worth the coordination overhead
Have the developer manually copy relevant findings into a new session before the modification phase begins
questions.explain:
Delegating the modification phase to a subagent that receives the exploration phase's key findings explicitly, while restricting its own toolset to what modification actually needs, preserves the continuity a fully separate, context-blind agent (the alternative being ruled out here) would lose, while still tightening tool access for the riskier, higher-precision phase.
Not “Keep a single agent and rely on prompt instructions to describe whi…” — Prompt instructions describing which tools to use do not change which tools are actually available, so the narrowing is not enforced.
Not “Run the whole task in one phase with all tools available throughout…” — Keeping all tools available throughout skips tightening access for the riskier modification phase, which is the aim.
Not “Have the developer manually copy relevant findings into a new sessi…” — Manually copying findings into a new session depends on the developer, risks omissions, and is far less reliable than an explicit handoff to a scoped subagent.

questions.q: A CI pipeline runs two independent jobs against the same PR: one does a general code review, the other runs a security-focused scan. Each spawns its own separate Claude Code invocation, and both happen to flag the same underlying issue (a missing null check on one specific line). Each job posts its own PR comment, so the same line gets two near-identical comments from two different "reviewers." Developers complain about the redundant notifications. What's the most effective way to prevent this specific kind of duplication?
options: Merge the two jobs into a single long-lived session so both sets of findings are produced together and can be reconciled before either is posted
Have whichever job runs second receive the first job's findings on the same PR as part of its input, with an instruction to skip anything the other job already flagged
Store every finding in a central datastore and run a deduplication pass across all findings from both jobs before anything is posted to GitHub
Force the two jobs to run strictly one after the other rather than in parallel, so the second can read a results file the first one wrote
questions.explain:
When two independent jobs can flag the same underlying issue, having the second job receive the first job's findings as input — with an explicit instruction to skip anything already flagged — removes the duplication at the source. Merging the jobs into one long-lived session creates the same kind of context-carryover risk seen elsewhere in CI reviews, and a purely infrastructure-level dedup pass is a heavier solution than simply passing the first job's output forward.
Not “Merge the two jobs into a single long-lived session so both sets of…” — Merging the jobs into one long-lived session allows context carryover between the general and security reviews and loses their independence.
Not “Store every finding in a central datastore and run a deduplication …” — A central datastore with a dedup pass is a heavier infrastructure approach than passing the first job's findings to the second.
Not “Force the two jobs to run strictly one after the other rather than …” — Forcing sequential runs alone does not stop duplicates unless the second job is told what the first already reported.

questions.q: A test-generation step produces unit tests referencing a fixture path like /opt/ci-fixtures/seed-data.json. These tests pass on every developer's local machine, but roughly 60% of them fail once run inside the containerized CI runner, where that absolute path doesn't exist. What's the most likely root cause, and the most direct fix?
options: The generated code assumes Unix-style paths; rewriting the tests to use Windows-style paths would resolve the CI failures

The test-generation prompt was never told that fixture paths must be relative to the repository root, and the project's CLAUDE.md doesn't document the test fixtures, helper utilities, or test-data layout actually available in the CI environment — so generation has no way to know the local absolute path won't exist there
CI containers mount volumes differently than developer machines; the fix belongs in the container configuration, not the generated tests
The test-generation step runs with context: fork, which is why it can't see the rest of the repository
questions.explain:
The generated tests fail in CI specifically because nothing available to the test-generation step describes the CI environment's actual fixture layout — the model has no way to know a developer-machine absolute path won't exist inside the container. Documenting the real fixture locations, helper utilities, and test-data structure in CLAUDE.md (or an equivalent always-loaded reference) gives every future invocation the information it's currently missing.
Not “The generated code assumes Unix-style paths; rewriting the tests to…” — The failure comes from the fixture path not existing in the container, not from Unix versus Windows path style.
Not “CI containers mount volumes differently than developer machines; th…” — Container mounts may differ, but the missing piece is that generation was never told the real fixture layout, which is why tests assume a local path.
Not “The test-generation step runs with context: fork, which is why it…” — context: fork is not shown to be involved. The tests fail because nothing documents the CI environment's fixtures for generation.

questions.q: A code-review job outputs structured findings (line_number, severity, description) via enforced JSON schema output. Reviewing a sample of findings, several reference line numbers well outside the actual range of lines the PR touched — for example, a finding at line 287 on a PR that only modified lines 42–156. These out-of-range findings still get posted as PR comments, where they read as irrelevant noise. What's the most reliable way to stop out-of-bounds findings from being posted?
options: Add an instruction to the review prompt: "only report findings within the changed lines of the diff"
Before posting each finding as a comment, validate its line_number against the PR diff's actual line range, and discard (or hold for manual review) anything that falls outside it
Switch to a larger model on the theory that it will have a better understanding of file scope
Lower the sampling temperature so line numbers come out "more precise"
questions.explain:
A prompt instruction to "only report changed lines" doesn't stop the model from generating a line number outside that range in the first place; validating each finding's line_number against the PR's actual diff bounds before posting is the deterministic check that actually filters out-of-range findings, rather than hoping instruction-following prevents them.
Not “Add an instruction to the review prompt: "only report findings with…” — A prompt instruction does not stop the model from emitting an out-of-range line number, so such findings can still appear.
Not “Switch to a larger model on the theory that it will have a better u…” — A larger model can still produce line numbers outside the diff, and it offers no deterministic guarantee that findings stay in range.
Not “Lower the sampling temperature so line numbers come out "more precise"” — Lower temperature affects randomness but does not bind the model to the diff's line range, so it cannot guarantee in-range findings.

questions.q: A .claude/rules/security.md file scoped with paths: ["src/**/*.ts"] contains guidance like "wrap all async operations in try/catch." Applied uniformly, this guidance also fires on test files such as src/auth.test.ts, where patterns like expect(promise).rejects.toThrow() are the idiomatic way to test a rejection and genuinely don't need a surrounding try/catch. Developers have started dismissing these findings as "doesn't apply to tests." What's the best way to separate production guidance from test-file guidance here?
options: Add an informal exception clause directly into the security guidance's prose: "...except in test files"

Add a second rule file scoped to test files specifically (e.g. paths: ["src/**/*.test.ts"]) containing test-aware guidance, so test files get conventions appropriate to tests instead of inheriting production-oriented rules wholesale
Remove all path-scoped rules and rely solely on a single root-level project memory file for every convention
Turn the security guidance off entirely until someone manually reviews every future finding
questions.explain:
A second rule file scoped specifically to test files lets test-appropriate conventions apply on their own terms, instead of inheriting a production-oriented rule (like mandatory try/catch wrapping) that doesn't fit idiomatic test patterns such as asserting on a rejected promise. This is more maintainable than an informal prose exception bolted onto the production rule, and it doesn't require giving up path-scoped guidance altogether.
Not “Add an informal exception clause directly into the security guidanc…” — A prose exception bolted onto the production rule is informal, can be ignored, and keeps test files inheriting guidance that does not fit them.
Not “Remove all path-scoped rules and rely solely on a single root-level…” — Removing path-scoped rules would lose the ability to apply conventions by file type, and a single root file brings back the bloat.
Not “Turn the security guidance off entirely until someone manually revi…” — Turning off the guidance gives up useful production checks entirely instead of separating the rules by file type.

questions.q: A test-generation prompt says "write thorough unit tests," and the resulting tests assert on implementation details — e.g. checking that a specific internal helper function was called a specific number of times — rather than on observable outcomes. The tests pass initially, but as soon as the implementation is reorganized (with identical external behavior), they break, generating churn complaints even though nothing user-facing changed. The prompt already includes "focus on behavior." What's the most effective next step?
options: Lower max_tokens to force shorter, and hopefully simpler, tests
Provide 2–3 concrete before/after examples contrasting an implementation-detail test with a behavior-driven test for the same function, and document the distinction as a standard in CLAUDE.md
Switch to a larger model, expecting it to have an inherently better grasp of testing philosophy
Have developers manually rewrite every generated test to remove implementation-detail assertions
questions.explain:
"Focus on behavior" alone hasn't resolved the ambiguity because "behavior" itself needs to be pinned down concretely; before/after examples contrasting an implementation-detail assertion with a behavior-driven one, documented as a standard, gives the model a concrete boundary to apply consistently — which a vague prose instruction, a smaller max_tokens budget, or a different model don't provide on their own.
Not “Lower max_tokens to force shorter, and hopefully simpler, tests” — max_tokens limits output length and does not tell the model to assert on outcomes rather than on internals, so tests stay brittle.
Not “Switch to a larger model, expecting it to have an inherently better…” — A larger model does not define what behaviour means for this codebase, so the ambiguity that produced the brittle tests would remain.
Not “Have developers manually rewrite every generated test to remove imp…” — Manually rewriting every generated test removes the automation benefit instead of fixing what the generator is told.

questions.q: A test-generation step is given the existing test file as context specifically to avoid creating duplicate tests. It still generates a new test with the exact same name as an existing one in that file — both are named identically. When the suite runs, the second definition silently overwrites the first, and the original test never executes again without anyone noticing. What's the most direct fix?
options: Run the test-generation step multiple times and have a developer manually reconcile any conflicts
Adopt a policy requiring every test name in the codebase to be globally unique, enforced by developer discipline
Include an explicit list of the existing test names already present in that file as part of the context, with an instruction to avoid reusing any of them
Disable test generation entirely for any file that already has existing tests
questions.explain:
The generation step already had the existing test file as context, but nothing told it those exact names were already taken; explicitly listing the existing test names and instructing the model to avoid reusing any of them gives it the specific information needed to prevent a silent, accidental name collision.
Not “Run the test-generation step multiple times and have a developer ma…” — Running generation repeatedly and having a developer reconcile conflicts adds manual work and still lets silent name collisions slip through.
Not “Adopt a policy requiring every test name in the codebase to be glob…” — A globally unique naming policy that relies on developer discipline is unenforced, and it does not give the generation step the names it must avoid.
Not “Disable test generation entirely for any file that already has exis…” — Disabling generation for files that already have tests loses valuable new coverage rather than just avoiding name collisions.

questions.q: A PostToolUse hook runs a code formatter after every file write, keeping the repository consistently formatted. A code-review job separately reads source files to analyze them and produce line-numbered findings as JSON. Because the review job's own file reads don't trigger the formatter, that's not the issue — instead, a separate process reformats the PR's files as part of an unrelated pre-review step, and the review job's line numbers, computed after that reformatting, no longer line up with the original PR diff's line numbers. Posted comments end up pointing at the wrong lines. What's the underlying issue, and the fix?
options: The review job should read from a snapshot of the files exactly as they existed in the PR diff, before any reformatting step touches them, so its line numbers stay aligned with what reviewers actually see in the diff
The formatter is changing line counts when it shouldn't; configure it to never alter line counts, even when reformatting
This is expected and unavoidable; the review prompt should instruct the model to guess at likely line-number drift
The review job needs a larger context window so it can somehow account for the reformatting on its own
questions.explain:
Once a separate process reformats the PR's files before review reads them, any line numbers the review computes are aligned to the reformatted version, not to the diff reviewers are actually looking at. Reading from a snapshot taken before that reformatting step keeps the review's line numbers aligned with the PR diff itself, which is what the posted comments need to match.
Not “The formatter is changing line counts when it shouldn't; configure …” — Forcing the formatter to preserve line counts is impractical and only addresses the symptom. The review should read the files as they appear in the diff.
Not “This is expected and unavoidable; the review prompt should instruct…” — Guessing at line-number drift is unreliable. The fix is to read from the original pre-reformatting version so the numbers match.
Not “The review job needs a larger context window so it can somehow acco…” — Window size has no effect on offsets introduced by an external reformatting step, so the line numbers would still be misaligned.

questions.q: A code-review tool call returns findings with fields including finding_type (an enum: bug / style / performance / security) and description (free text). Every finding passes schema validation — the JSON is well-formed and every field has a legal value. But some findings are miscategorized: a finding with finding_type: "security" has a description reading "variable naming could be more concise," which is clearly a style comment, not a security issue. This routes the finding to the wrong downstream review queue, and schema validation doesn't catch it. What's the most reliable fix?
options: Add more fine-grained values to the finding_type enum to reduce ambiguity between categories
Add a deterministic post-generation check that cross-references finding_type against keyword/pattern signals in description, flagging likely category mismatches before the finding is routed anywhere
Switch to a larger model on the assumption it will have better categorical judgment
Lower max_tokens to encourage more concise, and hopefully more accurate, categorization
questions.explain:
Schema validation only confirms the JSON is well-formed and each value is a legal enum member — it has no way to check whether the chosen category actually matches the finding's own description. A deterministic post-generation check that cross-references category against description content catches exactly this class of semantically-wrong-but-syntactically-valid output, which more enum granularity or a different model wouldn't reliably fix.
Not “Add more fine-grained values to the finding_type enum to reduce a…” — More enum values do not check that the chosen category matches the description, so a finding could still be labelled wrongly.
Not “Switch to a larger model on the assumption it will have better cate…” — A larger model may reduce mistakes but cannot guarantee correct categorisation, whereas a deterministic check catches mismatches reliably.
Not “Lower max_tokens to encourage more concise, and hopefully more ac…” — max_tokens limits length and has no effect on whether a category matches the finding's description.

questions.q: A test-generation job runs in a completely fresh session for each PR, producing tests that technically pass locally but consistently fail once merged into the team's CI suite — because they use generic ad hoc mocking instead of the repository's established test harness, custom fixtures, and helper utilities. The invocation only receives the changed code; none of the team's testing conventions or available utilities are documented anywhere the generation step can see them. What combination of changes would most improve generated test quality here?
options: Move testing guidance to an external wiki that developers are expected to read themselves; tests will improve once humans internalize the conventions

Document the team's testing conventions, available fixtures/helpers, and test-harness setup in CLAUDE.md so every test-generation invocation has that context available, and include a short example showing correct use of the existing test infrastructure
Restrict test generation to only the simplest, dependency-free utility functions
Stop using Claude Code for test generation on anything that depends on shared test infrastructure
questions.explain:
The generated tests fail in CI because nothing in the invocation describes the team's actual test infrastructure; documenting conventions, fixtures, and helpers in CLAUDE.md (giving every invocation that context) combined with a concrete example of correct usage (showing, not just telling, what "correct" looks like) directly targets the missing information, rather than relying on developers to catch it after the fact or restricting generation to only the simplest possible cases.
Not “Move testing guidance to an external wiki that developers are expec…” — An external wiki depends on humans reading it and is invisible to the test-generation step, so the generated tests keep using generic mocking.
Not “Restrict test generation to only the simplest, dependency-free util…” — Restricting generation to simple dependency-free functions avoids the problem instead of fixing it, and gives up useful coverage.
Not “Stop using Claude Code for test generation on anything that depends…” — Abandoning generation for code that uses shared infrastructure gives up value when the real fix is to document the infrastructure.

questions.q: An invoice-extraction pipeline using tool_use with a strict JSON schema produces syntactically valid JSON every time, but a downstream review flags that a vendor_name value like "Acme Corp" sometimes appears in the output even though no such name exists anywhere in the source document. The schema defines vendor_name as a required string. What change would most reliably catch this kind of hallucination going forward?
options: Lower the temperature to force more deterministic output
Make vendor_name nullable instead of required

Add a vendor_source_location field (e.g., "letterhead," "signature block," "table header," or null) documenting where in the source the vendor name was actually found, forcing the extraction to ground its claim in something checkable
Add a few-shot example that explicitly instructs the model not to hallucinate
questions.explain:
Schema validity only confirms the JSON is well-formed, not that a claimed value actually exists in the source. A vendor_source_location field forces the extraction to ground its claim in a specific, checkable part of the document — a null value there signals the vendor genuinely wasn't found, making hallucination visible in a way a required-but-ungrounded string field never was.
Not “Lower the temperature to force more deterministic output” — Lower temperature does not tie the value to the document, so the model can still output a name that never appears in the source.
Not “Make vendor_name nullable instead of required” — Making vendor_name nullable removes the pressure to invent a value but does not let you verify that a non-null value actually appears in the source.
Not “Add a few-shot example that explicitly instructs the model not to h…” — An example telling the model not to hallucinate is a probabilistic instruction, so it does not give a checkable guarantee.

questions.q: A contract-extraction pipeline has two tools: one for prose clauses, one for tabular terms. Many real contracts contain both. The two tool descriptions currently say one extracts "contract text" and the other extracts "document tables," but in practice the model tends to call only one of the two tools even on documents that clearly contain both prose and tables. What's the most direct fix?
options: Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool
Rewrite both descriptions to clearly state which data each tool covers, and explicitly note that documents containing both prose and tables should trigger both tools in sequence
Force tool_choice to a single specific named tool
Add a preprocessing step that physically splits every document into separate table-only and prose-only files before extraction
questions.explain:
Tool descriptions are the primary signal driving selection; when they're vague about scope and silent on documents that need both tools, the model has no reason to call more than one. Making the descriptions explicit about what each covers — and stating outright that a document with both prose and tables should trigger both — directly addresses the observed under-calling, ahead of merging the tools or forcing a single named tool.
Not “Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool” — Merging the tools hides the distinction between prose and tables and does not fix the underlying issue, which is unclear descriptions.
Not “Force tool_choice to a single specific named tool” — Forcing one specific tool would guarantee the other is never called, making under-extraction worse.
Not “Add a preprocessing step that physically splits every document into…” — Splitting every document into table-only and prose-only files adds a complicated preprocessing step when clearer descriptions would solve it.

questions.q: A team processes 40 vendor invoices as a single long batch within one conversation. The first 10 or so extract cleanly, but starting partway through the batch, later invoices begin returning vendor names, account numbers, or reference codes that actually belong to an earlier invoice in the same batch, not the one currently being extracted. What change would most reliably eliminate this cross-document carryover?
options: Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to extract carefully
Split the batch into independent single-invoice extraction calls instead of processing all 40 within one shared conversation
Add a scratchpad listing every vendor and reference number seen so far, instructing the model to avoid reusing any value already on the list
Lower the model's temperature
questions.explain:
Processing all 40 invoices inside one shared conversation lets details from earlier documents bleed into later extractions as context accumulates — splitting the batch into independent, single-invoice calls removes the shared context that's causing the carryover entirely, rather than just narrowing it (as a scratchpad, C, would) or hoping more tokens or a lower temperature changes the underlying behavior.
Not “Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to extract carefully” — max_tokens limits output length and does not stop earlier invoices' details from bleeding into later extractions.
Not “Add a scratchpad listing every vendor and reference number seen so …” — A list of values seen so far only narrows the problem and grows with the batch, while the shared accumulating context remains.
Not “Lower the model's temperature” — Lower temperature does not remove the shared conversation context that is causing earlier invoices to affect later ones.

questions.q: A purchase-order extraction schema requires a po_number field and also has a document_type enum ("purchase_order" | "invoice" | "quote"). In practice, many documents get classified as "purchase_order" even though they're actually invoices that never contained a PO number at all — and validation, which runs only after the full extraction is returned, then fails on the missing po_number. What change would most reliably improve accuracy here?
options: Keep retrying the same prompt until validation happens to pass
Make po_number nullable so invoices no longer fail validation, while keeping document_type required as-is
Restructure extraction into two steps: first classify the document type from its structure/headers, then only require po_number when that first step actually confirms the document is a purchase order
Drop the po_number requirement from the schema entirely
questions.explain:
Since whether po_number should even be expected depends entirely on the document actually being a purchase order, classifying the document type first and only then conditionally requiring po_number prevents the mismatch from ever reaching validation, instead of discovering it only after the full extraction already ran or giving up the requirement across the board.
Not “Keep retrying the same prompt until validation happens to pass” — Retrying the same prompt does not fix a misclassified document, and a retry could just fail the same way repeatedly.
Not “Make po_number nullable so invoices no longer fail validation, wh…” — Making the field nullable removes the validation failure but does not fix the misclassification of invoices as purchase orders.
Not “Drop the po_number requirement from the schema entirely” — Dropping po_number entirely loses the field for documents that really are purchase orders.

questions.q: A contract-extraction schema has a required contract_start_date field. Some contracts state both an "executed date" (when the parties signed) and a separate "effective date" (when obligations actually begin), and these differ. The model picks inconsistently between the two across otherwise-similar contracts, and adding a couple of generic few-shot examples hasn't resolved the inconsistency. What's the next step?
options: Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to reason about which date to pick
Merge both dates into a single freeform text field instead of picking one

Add few-shot examples that include the explicit reasoning for the choice (e.g., "when both dates appear, prefer the effective date, since that's when obligations actually begin") plus a schema-level comment stating that precedence rule directly
Switch to a larger model and hope it infers the right precedence on its own
questions.explain:
Generic before/after examples weren't enough because they didn't convey *why* one date should be preferred over the other; adding the explicit precedence reasoning to the examples, backed by a schema-level comment stating the same rule, gives the model a concrete, repeatable basis for the choice instead of leaving it to infer a pattern from examples alone.
Not “Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to reason about w…” — More max_tokens allows longer output but does not tell the model which date should take precedence.
Not “Merge both dates into a single freeform text field instead of picki…” — A free-text field combining both dates loses the structured start date that the schema needs and does not resolve which one counts.
Not “Switch to a larger model and hope it infers the right precedence on…” — A larger model has no way of knowing the team's precedence rule unless it is stated, so inconsistency may persist.

questions.q: Two extraction tools, one for pulling out defined terms from a contract and one for pulling out the parties' actual obligations, both currently have descriptions that vaguely claim to cover "important contract terms." Developers have observed that the terms-extraction tool is sometimes relied on to also capture obligations, leading to silently incomplete extractions when it doesn't. What's the most effective first fix?
options: Rewrite both descriptions to explicitly separate their scope — state precisely what each tool does and doesn't cover, with a short example for each, so the overlap in "important contract terms" no longer blurs the boundary
Force the pipeline to always call both tools on every document regardless of content
Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool
Add a validation check after extraction that tries to detect whether obligations are missing from the output
questions.explain:
Both tools currently describe themselves with the same vague phrase ("important contract terms"), which is exactly what's letting one substitute for the other. Rewriting the descriptions to state precisely what each does and doesn't cover, with an example apiece, removes the ambiguity directly — well ahead of forcing both tools to always run or merging them outright, which gives up the distinction the team wants to keep.
Not “Force the pipeline to always call both tools on every document rega…” — Always calling both tools wastes effort on documents that only need one, and it does not clarify what each covers.
Not “Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool” — Merging the tools gives up the distinction the team wants between defined terms and obligations.
Not “Add a validation check after extraction that tries to detect whethe…” — A check after extraction detects missing obligations late and does not fix the ambiguous descriptions causing the substitution.

questions.q: A team processes 500 supplier invoices every business day and wants to move extraction to the Message Batches API to capture a meaningful cost discount. Current same-day processing takes about 2 hours from submission. Downstream financial-close processes need results by 9 AM the next business day. The Batches API carries no latency SLA and can, in the worst case, take up to 24 hours. If a batch is submitted at 6 PM, what's the latest it might reasonably return under that worst case, and what does that imply?
options: Always by 8 AM the next morning, so the move is safe as planned

As late as 6 PM the following day (24 hours after submission) in the worst case — which would blow past the 9 AM downstream deadline entirely, meaning this workflow shouldn't rely on the Batches API for its full volume without a real fallback plan
Within roughly 2 hours, the same as the current synchronous process
There's a documented, guaranteed 18-hour turnaround specifically for financial workloads
questions.explain:
With no latency SLA, a 6 PM submission could in the worst case take the full 24 hours, landing right around 6 PM the following day — well past the 9 AM downstream deadline. Treating "up to 24 hours" as if it were a guaranteed same-morning turnaround or assuming it behaves like the current 2-hour synchronous process both mistake an unbounded worst case for a reliable one.
Not “Always by 8 AM the next morning, so the move is safe as planned” — There is no guarantee of an overnight finish. Without a latency SLA, a batch submitted at 6 PM could take much longer than until 8 AM.
Not “Within roughly 2 hours, the same as the current synchronous process” — Batch processing does not behave like the current synchronous process, and its completion time is not bounded by two hours.
Not “There's a documented, guaranteed 18-hour turnaround specifically fo…” — The Batches API has no documented guaranteed turnaround for financial or any other workloads, only a worst-case window.

questions.q: A vendor-management schema classifies every vendor with an enum: "supplier" | "contractor" | "service_provider" | "reseller". In practice, some real vendor relationships (joint ventures, co-managed partnerships, regional distributor arrangements) don't cleanly fit any of the four categories, and the model is forced into a misclassification every time one comes up. What schema change best handles this kind of long-tail extensibility?
options: Drop the enum constraint entirely and make vendor_category a free-text string
Add an "other" value to the enum, plus an optional vendor_category_detail string field for a free-text explanation whenever "other" is chosen
Create an entirely separate extraction tool for every additional vendor type as it's discovered
Add a confidence score to the category field and route anything below a threshold to manual review, without changing the enum itself
questions.explain:
An "other" enum value paired with a free-text detail field lets the schema stay structured and queryable for the common cases while still accommodating the genuine long tail of relationships that don't fit any predefined category — without either abandoning structure entirely or requiring a brand-new tool every time a new edge case appears.
Not “Drop the enum constraint entirely and make vendor_category a free…” — Dropping the enum for free text loses the structure and consistency of a fixed set, making categories harder to query and compare.
Not “Create an entirely separate extraction tool for every additional ve…” — Creating a new tool for every extra vendor type does not scale and means rewriting the pipeline repeatedly for edge cases.
Not “Add a confidence score to the category field and route anything bel…” — Routing low-confidence results to manual review leaves the enum unable to represent these relationships, so misclassifications continue.

questions.q: Six months into production, a team wants to analyze why certain extractions get rejected by downstream reviewers. Current logs record only document_id, field_name, extracted_value, and a final disposition of accepted or rejected — nothing about the document itself. The team suspects failures cluster around things like poor-quality scans, handwritten amounts, very long multi-page contracts where key terms appear late in the document, or particular vendor formats, but the existing logs give no way to confirm or prioritize any of that. What should be added to enable real root-cause analysis?
options: A random UUID per extraction, purely for tracing a record back to its source document

Structured document metadata logged alongside each extraction — source type (scanned vs. native), an OCR-quality signal where applicable, page count, and roughly where in the document the field was found — so rejections can be correlated with the actual characteristics of the input that produced them
A separate machine-learning model trained specifically to predict which documents are likely to fail
A recurring manual review of a random sample of rejections, done by hand, to look for patterns
questions.explain:
Logging the actual characteristics of the input alongside each extraction — scan quality, page count, roughly where in the document a field was found — is what makes it possible to correlate rejections with real causes (a long contract, a poor scan, a particular vendor's layout) instead of treating every rejection as an undifferentiated data point with nothing to explain it.
Not “A random UUID per extraction, purely for tracing a record back to i…” — A random UUID lets you trace a record back to its document, but says nothing about the document's characteristics that might explain rejections.
Not “A separate machine-learning model trained specifically to predict w…” — Training a separate prediction model is heavy and premature when basic input characteristics have not even been logged yet.
Not “A recurring manual review of a random sample of rejections, done by…” — Reviewing a random sample by hand is slow and does not scale, and without recorded input characteristics there is little to correlate.

questions.q: Your resolution agent must check customer account status and recent order history before acting on a case. The two lookups have no ordering dependency on each other, but the coordinator currently dispatches them as two sequential subagent calls, and high case volume is making that round-trip latency a real bottleneck. What's the most effective fix?
options: Merge both lookups into a single combined subagent that performs both investigations in one turn
Emit both Task calls within a single coordinator response so the two subagents run concurrently, then collect both results before proceeding
Add a batching layer that packs multiple subagent invocations into one API request
Increase max_tokens so each lookup resolves faster
questions.explain:
Emitting both Task calls within a single coordinator response is what actually runs the two subagents concurrently; merging them into one subagent loses the modularity of separate investigations, and neither a generic batching layer nor a bigger token budget changes the fact that the calls are currently dispatched sequentially.
Not “Merge both lookups into a single combined subagent that performs bo…” — Merging the lookups into one subagent loses the modularity of separate investigations, and it does not run two subagents side by side.
Not “Add a batching layer that packs multiple subagent invocations into …” — A generic batching layer packs requests together but does not make the two independent subagent calls run concurrently from the coordinator.
Not “Increase max_tokens so each lookup resolves faster” — max_tokens limits output length. It does not change that the calls are dispatched one after another, which is the actual bottleneck.

questions.q: Your refund tool exposes refund_reason_code (an enum: "defective," "not_as_described," "customer_request," "policy_exception") and refund_justification (free text for additional context). Logs show the agent frequently stuffs long explanatory text into reason_code and leaves justification blank, even on cases where a bare code isn't enough detail for the finance team to evaluate. Both parameters already have descriptions. What's the clearest next fix?
options: Rename both parameters to something else entirely, on the theory that new names alone will resolve the confusion
Merge them into a single free-text refund_reason field and parse category and detail out of it server-side

Expand both parameter descriptions with concrete guidance: reason_code gets "must be exactly one of the enum values, never free text"; justification gets an example of what to write when the code alone doesn't capture enough context
Add a hook that rejects the call outright whenever justification is empty
questions.explain:
Concrete guidance in the description — exactly what belongs in the enum vs. what belongs in free text, with an example of when justification is actually needed — is the direct, lowest-effort fix for this kind of field-misuse pattern, ahead of renaming, merging the fields, or bolting on a rejection hook.
Not “Rename both parameters to something else entirely, on the theory th…” — Renaming parameters alone does nothing to clarify what belongs in the enum versus the free text, so the same misuse would continue.
Not “Merge them into a single free-text refund_reason field and parse …” — A single free-text field gives up the enum's structure and moves parsing to the server, which is a heavier fix for a simple description problem.
Not “Add a hook that rejects the call outright whenever justification …” — A rejection hook on empty justification forces text even when none is needed and does not teach the agent what belongs where.

questions.q: A customer disputes charges across three orders plus one account-level adjustment, requesting a $620 total refund. An initial lookup surfaces all four transaction amounts. After two subagents separately investigate return eligibility and account reconciliation, the synthesis step produces a final recommendation of "approve $105" — referencing the adjustment but dropping the three order amounts entirely, even though both subagents' own outputs were correct and complete. What's the most direct fix?
options: Increase the context window so intermediate results never need to be summarized
Maintain a persistent "case facts" block (each transaction ID and amount) carried alongside every prompt, outside the part of the conversation that gets condensed into a narrative summary
Re-run both subagent investigations at a higher temperature for more thorough coverage
Have the customer restate all four disputed amounts before the agent finalizes anything
questions.explain:
A persistent case-facts block carried outside the part of the conversation that gets condensed is what keeps specific numbers from disappearing during synthesis, which is exactly what happened to three of the four transaction amounts here. A bigger context window doesn't stop summarization from happening; higher temperature adds noise, not fidelity; and asking the customer to repeat themselves is a workaround, not a fix.
Not “Increase the context window so intermediate results never need to b…” — A larger context window does not prevent summarisation from happening, and the amounts were lost in condensing, not for lack of space.
Not “Re-run both subagent investigations at a higher temperature for mor…” — Higher temperature adds randomness rather than fidelity, so it would not keep the three order amounts in the final recommendation.
Not “Have the customer restate all four disputed amounts before the agen…” — Asking the customer to restate the amounts shifts the burden onto them and does not fix the loss of figures during synthesis.

questions.q: Your single general-purpose resolution agent handles returns, billing disputes, and account-security cases, with access to every relevant tool across all three areas. First-contact resolution varies sharply by category: returns succeed 88% of the time, billing disputes only 59%, and account-security cases are occasionally escalated based on insufficient identity verification depth. What's the most effective structural fix?
options: Give the single agent even more tools, including advanced financial-analysis and multi-factor-auth capabilities

Introduce a lightweight intake step that classifies each case and routes it to a specialized subagent per category (returns, billing, security), each scoped to only the tools relevant to its own case type
Keep one general agent, but add 15+ few-shot examples spanning all three case types
Split the system into three fully separate backend services, one per case type, with no shared coordinator at all
questions.explain:
Routing each case to a specialized subagent scoped to only its own category's tools directly addresses uneven performance across very different case types, without expanding any single agent's tool surface or relying on examples alone to cover three very different domains. Splitting into fully separate backend services throws away the shared coordinator without actually fixing tool scoping.
Not “Give the single agent even more tools, including advanced financial…” — Adding more tools to one agent increases its decision surface, which tends to worsen selection rather than improve uneven performance across categories.
Not “Keep one general agent, but add 15+ few-shot examples spanning all …” — Fifteen examples spread across three very different domains do not narrow the agent's tools, and the uneven results come from covering everything in one agent.
Not “Split the system into three fully separate backend services, one pe…” — Three entirely separate services with no coordinator removes the shared routing and oversight without solving how tools are scoped per case type.

questions.q: escalate_to_human is meant to always carry structured context (customer ID, root cause, attempted actions), and the system prompt says so explicitly and emphatically. Logs still show a meaningful share of escalations going out with minimal or blank context, and the coordinator doesn't stop them. What's the most direct, deterministic fix?
options: Make the system-prompt wording even stronger and more emphatic
Define escalate_to_human's input schema so customer_id, root_cause, and attempted_actions are required parameters the call cannot be made without
Add a hook that inspects the call after the fact and flags escalations with thin context for follow-up
Split escalate_to_human into two separate tools, one for routine escalations and one for emergencies
questions.explain:
Making the required fields part of the tool's own input schema means the call literally cannot be made without them — a deterministic guarantee that stronger prompt wording or a hook that only flags problems after the fact can't provide. Splitting the tool in two doesn't address the missing-context problem itself.
Not “Make the system-prompt wording even stronger and more emphatic” — Stronger wording is still advisory. The prompt already says this emphatically, yet escalations keep going out without context.
Not “Add a hook that inspects the call after the fact and flags escalati…” — A hook that only flags thin escalations afterward lets them go out first, so it does not prevent the missing context.
Not “Split escalate_to_human into two separate tools, one for routine …” — Splitting the tool into routine and emergency versions does nothing about the missing customer_id, root_cause and attempted_actions.

questions.q: Your written policy explicitly covers defective items (90-day window) and wrong items shipped (30-day window), but says nothing about unopened, resalable items returned outside either window — a real request that comes up in about 5% of cases. The agent currently escalates every one of these, which is dragging down first-contact resolution, even though the policy's spirit plausibly supports approving some of them. Under what condition should a case like this actually go to a human?
options: Whenever it involves more than one order or a large dollar amount
When the agent has genuinely run out of applicable policy to reason from — the request falls into real silence or ambiguity in the documented rules — and further tool calls won't resolve that gap
Once the agent has made at least three tool calls, since that indicates a thorough-enough investigation
Whenever sentiment analysis on the customer's message indicates frustration or urgency
questions.explain:
The right trigger for escalation is a genuine gap or silence in the documented policy that no further investigation can resolve on its own — not proxies like order count, dollar amount, tool-call count, or sentiment, all of which correlate poorly with whether the agent is actually equipped to decide the case.
Not “Whenever it involves more than one order or a large dollar amount” — Order count and dollar amount are proxies that do not show whether the policy covers the case, so they would send some solvable cases to humans.
Not “Once the agent has made at least three tool calls, since that indic…” — Tool-call count measures effort, not whether a policy gap exists, so it would escalate or hold cases for the wrong reasons.
Not “Whenever sentiment analysis on the customer's message indicates fru…” — Frustration or urgency does not indicate that policy is silent, so sentiment would escalate cases the agent can resolve.

questions.q: A pilot workflow needs three sequential checks — eligibility, account reconciliation, fraud assessment — where a red flag at any step should escalate immediately rather than continuing to the next step. The current coordinator runs all three regardless, and only checks for red flags once every step has already finished, wasting effort on cases that should have escalated at step one. What's the best fix?
options: Bake a rigid, fully-enumerated if-then-else decision tree directly into the coordinator's prompt
Have the coordinator inspect each subagent's result before dispatching the next one, and escalate immediately the moment a red flag appears, instead of always running the full sequence
Remove the subagent layer and have one agent call all the underlying tools directly with branching logic
Run all three checks in parallel, then escalate afterward if any of them raised a flag
questions.explain:
Checking each step's result before dispatching the next lets the coordinator escalate the moment a red flag appears, instead of always paying for every remaining step regardless of outcome. A rigid pre-baked decision tree is brittle against cases outside its exact enumerated conditions, and running everything in parallel doesn't save any of the wasted work this fix is meant to eliminate.
Not “Bake a rigid, fully-enumerated if-then-else decision tree directly …” — A rigid pre-written decision tree is brittle against cases outside its enumerated conditions and does not itself check results between steps.
Not “Remove the subagent layer and have one agent call all the underlyin…” — Removing the subagent layer in favour of one agent with branching logic gives up modular investigation without solving the early-exit problem.
Not “Run all three checks in parallel, then escalate afterward if any of…” — Running all three checks in parallel still pays for every check before any flag is acted on, so it saves none of the wasted work.

questions.q: A subagent tasked with verifying a customer's shipping address calls an address-validation tool twice; both attempts time out. It returns {"status": "complete", "findings": "Address verification unavailable"}. The coordinator reads this as "verification succeeded, address is fine" and proceeds to process the refund — but the address was actually wrong, and the shipment later fails. What's the core issue, and the fix?
options: The subagent's retry logic is too conservative; it should keep retrying until the backend eventually responds

The subagent needs a way to clearly distinguish "I investigated and got a definitive answer" from "I was unable to investigate at all," using a distinct status or explicit failure marker — so the coordinator can't mistake an inability to verify for a successful verification
Address validation is too unreliable to be part of this workflow and should be removed
The coordinator should automatically escalate any case where address data comes back unavailable
questions.explain:
The subagent needs a way to say "I could not verify this" that's structurally distinct from "I verified this and it's fine" — without that distinction, the coordinator has no way to avoid treating an inability to check as a clean pass. Retrying indefinitely doesn't solve the reporting problem, dropping the check loses real value, and blanket auto-escalation overcorrects for a problem that's really about signal clarity.
Not “The subagent's retry logic is too conservative; it should keep retr…” — Retrying until the backend responds could stall indefinitely, and it still would not tell the coordinator whether verification actually happened.
Not “Address validation is too unreliable to be part of this workflow an…” — Removing address validation loses real value. The issue is that a failure was reported as a completed check, not that the check exists.
Not “The coordinator should automatically escalate any case where addres…” — Escalating every case with unavailable address data overcorrects. The core problem is that the coordinator cannot tell failure from success.

questions.q: A complex billing dispute has two defensible outcomes given the exact same underlying facts (verified identity, order history, account status): a strict-policy calculation of $280, and a goodwill-exception calculation of $420. You want to reason through both paths independently — without one path's assumptions contaminating the other — but re-verifying the same facts from scratch in two completely separate sessions wastes backend calls and risks the two paths ending up with subtly inconsistent fact bases. What approach best threads this needle?
