questions.q: Two extraction tools — one for software license agreements, one for software purchase orders — both have clear, detailed descriptions with examples and non-examples. Documents that are genuinely both at once (e.g., "we are purchasing 50 seats of Software X under the following license terms...") still get routed to the wrong single tool often enough to cause schema mismatches, and neither more prompt clarification nor more few-shot examples has closed the gap. What architectural change would most reliably handle documents that are genuinely, structurally ambiguous like this?
options: Add an explicit document-type classification step first — licensing, purchase, or hybrid — and route based on that classification's result rather than asking either extraction tool to also do double duty as a classifier
Switch from tool_choice: "any" to "auto" so the model can decline to extract at all if it's unsure
Force tool_choice to always select one specific tool (say, the purchase-order tool) regardless of content
Merge both tools into a single, multi-purpose extraction tool
questions.explain:
When a document is genuinely, structurally both things at once, no amount of sharpening either extraction tool's own description will fully resolve the ambiguity, because the ambiguity is a property of the document, not the tool definitions; an explicit classification step (including a genuine "hybrid" outcome) that then routes accordingly is what actually handles that case, rather than asking one of the two extraction tools to also silently double as a classifier.
Not “Switch from tool_choice: "any" to "auto" so the model can decli…” — Switching to "auto" would allow the model to skip extraction altogether, giving up the guarantee while not resolving the hybrid document problem.
Not “Force tool_choice to always select one specific tool (say, the pu…” — Forcing one tool would apply the purchase-order schema to licence-only documents and miss licence terms, causing more mismatches.
Not “Merge both tools into a single, multi-purpose extraction tool” — Merging both tools bloats one schema and loses the distinct fields each type needs, instead of recognising hybrid documents.

questions.q: A team processes 8,000 invoices daily. Processing currently kicks off at 2 PM and results must be loaded into the accounting system by 5 PM the same day — a roughly 3-hour window. A cost-reduction proposal suggests moving this workload to the Message Batches API to capture a real cost discount. Is this workflow, as currently timed, a good fit?
options: Yes — process the full daily batch via the Batches API; the window will comfortably cover it
Partially — only use the Batches API for the portion submitted early enough in the day that a worst-case delay still lands before 5 PM, and keep the rest on synchronous calls

No — the Batches API has no latency SLA and can, in the worst case, take up to 24 hours; that's fundamentally incompatible with a same-day, hard-deadline workflow like this one, so it should stay on synchronous calls entirely
Yes, but only if every individual invoice document stays under a certain file size
questions.explain:
With no latency SLA and a documented worst case of up to 24 hours, the Batches API is fundamentally incompatible with a hard same-day deadline like this one — treating "up to 24 hours" as something that will comfortably fit inside a 3-hour window misunderstands what "no SLA" actually means, and a partial migration for only the earliest-submitted invoices still leaves the same unbounded risk for whatever doesn't make that early cutoff.
Not “Yes — process the full daily batch via the Batches API; the window …” — With no latency guarantee and a worst case of up to 24 hours, the batch cannot be relied on to finish within a three-hour window.
Not “Partially — only use the Batches API for the portion submitted earl…” — Partial migration still leaves the same unbounded delay risk for whatever is batched, so deadlines could still be missed.
Not “Yes, but only if every individual invoice document stays under a ce…” — File size is not what makes batch unsuitable. The disqualifying factor is the missing latency guarantee against a hard same-day deadline.

questions.q: A schema extracts procurement data from both supplier quotes and purchase orders, and adds a new bulk_discount_percentage field meant to apply to both — but many real quotes and purchase orders simply don't have a bulk discount at all. Because the field is marked required, the model fabricates a plausible discount percentage whenever the source document doesn't actually mention one. What change most directly fixes this?
options: Make the field optional/nullable, so its genuine absence in a source document no longer forces the model to invent a value
Change the field to a free-text string that can describe a discount in prose, e.g. "10% off for bulk orders"
Build entirely separate schemas for quotes and purchase orders, each handling discounts independently
Remove the field from the schema and compute any discount downstream from other extracted values instead
questions.explain:
When a field is genuinely and legitimately absent from many real source documents, making it nullable is what stops the model from having to invent a value just to satisfy a required-field constraint — separate schemas per document type don't address the actual mismatch (discount data that's optional within a single document type, not just across types), and a free-text field or removing it downstream both give up structure the pipeline still needs.
Not “Change the field to a free-text string that can describe a discount…” — A free-text string loses the numeric structure the pipeline needs and still does not remove the pressure to write something for a required field.
Not “Build entirely separate schemas for quotes and purchase orders, eac…” — Separate schemas per document type do not fix the problem, since many documents of both types lack a discount.
Not “Remove the field from the schema and compute any discount downstrea…” — Removing the field and computing discounts downstream discards data that is stated in some documents and can only be derived with guesswork.

questions.q: A team processes 4,000 invoices weekly and already categorizes extraction errors by type — "date format inconsistency" (6%), "currency mismatch" (4%), "line-item count off by one" (3%) — but has no way to tell whether, say, date errors cluster around handwritten invoices, particular vendors, particular countries, or scanned-vs-native documents. That makes it hard to know where to actually invest effort on the prompt or validation rules. What should be added to the structured output to make that kind of root-cause analysis possible?
options: A random UUID attached to each extraction, purely for tracing a record back to its source

A source_metadata field recording document characteristics alongside each extraction — format (handwritten/scanned/digital), an OCR-confidence signal where relevant, vendor name, and vendor country — so errors can actually be grouped and analyzed by the characteristics of the input that produced them
A free-text note field where the model can explain its own extraction in its own words
A counter tracking how many retries a given extraction needed before it succeeded
questions.explain:
Logging the actual characteristics of the document alongside each extraction — format, OCR confidence where relevant, vendor, country — is what turns three flat error-rate percentages into something that can actually be correlated with a root cause, which a bare trace ID, a free-text note, or a retry counter don't provide on their own.
Not “A random UUID attached to each extraction, purely for tracing a rec…” — A random UUID lets you trace a record to its source but says nothing about the document's characteristics, so errors cannot be grouped.
Not “A free-text note field where the model can explain its own extracti…” — A free-text note in the model's own words is unstructured and cannot be aggregated to show which document characteristics correlate with errors.
Not “A counter tracking how many retries a given extraction needed befor…” — A retry counter shows effort needed but not why an extraction failed, so it cannot reveal clusters by vendor, country or format.
